maths-2014-ol-p1-q7-b-iii.description: Mary wishes to buy a new car, which costs €24 000, on the 1st July 2014. Option (i): Buy Right Car Sales offers Mary €10 500 for her old car. At the end of the six months Mary would make a payment of €4000 and would be charged interest at a compound rate of 1·5% per month for the next six months. How much would Mary repay on 1st July 2015? Which of the above options should Mary choose if she wishes to pay the least amount? Justify your answer by calculation.

Percentage of registered homeowners: €0–€100 000, 24·9%; €100 001–€150 000, 28·6%; €150 001–€200 000, 21·9%; €200 001–€250 000, 10·4%; €250 001–€300 000, 4·9%; over €300 000, 9·3%. Tax per property by valuation band: €0–€100 000: €45; €100 001–€150 000: €112; €150 001–€200 000: €157; €200 001–€250 000: €202; €250 001–€300 000: €247; over €300 000: NA. The table gives 425 790 properties and €19 160 550 total tax for the first band, and 489 060 properties for the second. NA = Not Available. The total tax due on all the properties that were registered was estimated at €241 million. Find the mean estimated tax per property on those properties with a valuation over €300 000.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q7-c-v.description: A newspaper report in October 2013 stated that 90% of homeowners who were liable for property tax had registered for it. The total number of properties liable for the tax was estimated at 1·9 million. Homeowners, who registered, were required to value their property in one of a number of given Valuation Bands. Percentage of registered homeowners: €0–€100 000, 24·9%; €100 001–€150 000, 28·6%; €150 001–€200 000, 21·9%; €200 001–€250 000, 10·4%; €250 001–€300 000, 4·9%; over €300 000, 9·3%. Tax per property by valuation band: €0–€100 000: €45; €100 001–€150 000: €112; €150 001–€200 000: €157; €200 001–€250 000: €202; €250 001–€300 000: €247; over €300 000: NA. The table gives 425 790 properties and €19 160 550 total tax for the first band, and 489 060 properties for the second. NA = Not Available. Some homeowners may under-value their property in order to pay less tax. For example, one estimate stated that 20% of properties in the €100 001–€150 000 band should have been valued in the €150 001–€200 000 band. Based on this estimate, find the amount of extra tax that would be raised if these properties were registered in the correct Valuation Band.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q8-a-i.description: A wind turbine, used to generate electricity, has three equally spaced blades 65 metres long. Write down the size of the angle between two blades.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q8-a-iii.description: A wind turbine, used to generate electricity, has three equally spaced blades 65 metres long. Find the area of the triangle formed by joining the tips of the three blades, correct to the nearest whole number.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q8-b.description: Gráinne stood at a point B, which is on level ground 100 metres from the base of the tower supporting the blades, as shown. From there, she measured the angle of elevation to the top of the tower as 60°. Find the height of the tower, using Gráinne’s measurements. Give your answer correct to the nearest metre.

From there, she measured the angle of elevation to the top of the tower as 60°. Gráinne recognises that her measurement of the angle may not be totally accurate. She read elsewhere that the actual height of the tower is 154 m. If Gráinne measured the 100 m accurately, find the actual size of the angle at B, correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q8-c-ii.description: Gráinne stood at a point B, which is on level ground 100 metres from the base of the tower supporting the blades, as shown. She read elsewhere that the actual height of the tower is 154 m. Part (c)(i): Find the actual size of the angle at B, correct to the nearest degree. Find the percentage error in Gráinne’s measurement of the angle of elevation, correct to one decimal place.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q9-a-i.description: At an activity centre a zip-line, [BD], runs between two vertical poles, [AB] and [CD], on level ground, as shown. The point E is on the ground, directly below the zip-line. |AE| = 12 m, |BE| = 14 m, |CD| = 1·95 m, and |EC| = 10 m. Find the distance |ED|, correct to one decimal place.

The point E is on the ground, directly below the zip-line. |AE| = 12 m, |BE| = 14 m, |CD| = 1·95 m, and |EC| = 10 m. Find |∠AEB|, correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q9-b-i.description: At an activity centre a zip-line, [BD], runs between two vertical poles, [AB] and [CD], on level ground, as shown. The point E is on the ground, directly below the zip-line. |AE| = 12 m, |BE| = 14 m, |CD| = 1·95 m, and |EC| = 10 m. Find |∠DEB|, given that |∠CED| = 11°, correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q9-b-ii.description: At an activity centre a zip-line, [BD], runs between two vertical poles, [AB] and [CD], on level ground, as shown. maths-2014-ol-p2-q1-a-i.description: A garage has 5 black cars, 9 red cars and 10 silver cars for sale. A car is selected at random. What is the probability that: (i) The car is black? (ii) The car is black or red?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q1-b-i.description: A garage has 5 black cars, 9 red cars and 10 silver cars for sale. A car is selected at random. Then a second car is selected at random from those remaining. What is the probability that the first car is silver and the second car is black?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q1-b-ii.description: A garage has 5 black cars, 9 red cars and 10 silver cars for sale. A car is selected at random. Then a second car is selected at random from those remaining. What is the probability that one of the selected cars is red and the other is black?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q1-c.description: A garage has 5 black cars, 9 red cars and 10 silver cars for sale. Three of the black cars, two of the red cars and four of the silver cars have diesel engines. One car from the garage is again selected at random. What is the probability that it is a red car or a diesel car?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q2-a.description: When taking a penalty kick, the probability that Kevin scores is always 3/4. Kevin takes a penalty. What is the probability that he does not score?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q2-b.description: When taking a penalty kick, the probability that Kevin scores is always 3/4. Kevin takes two penalties. What is the probability that he scores both?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q2-c.description: When taking a penalty kick, the probability that Kevin scores is always 3/4. Kevin takes three penalties. What is the probability that he scores exactly twice?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q2-d.description: When taking a penalty kick, the probability that Kevin scores is always 3/4. Kevin takes five penalties. What is the probability that he scores for the first time on his fifth penalty?

maths-2014-ol-p2-q3-a-i.description: The circle c has equation (x + 2)² + (y − 3)² = 100. (i) Write down the co-ordinates of A, the centre of c. Write down r, the length of the radius of c. (ii) Show that the point P(−8, 11) is on the circle c.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q4-a-i.description: The points A(−9, 3), B(−4, 3) and C(−4, 10) are the vertices of the triangle ABC, as shown. Find the length of [AB].

(i) Draw, on the diagram above, a triangle, XYZ, which is congruent to the triangle ABC. (ii) Write down the co-ordinates of Z and explain why the triangle XYZ is congruent to the triangle ABC.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q6a-a-i.description: Construct the incircle of the triangle ABC below. Show all your construction lines clearly.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q7-a-i.description: A newspaper report in October 2013 stated that 90% of homeowners who were liable for property tax had registered for it. The total number of properties liable for the tax was estimated at 1·9 million. (i) Estimate the number of properties that were registered. (ii) Suggest one reason why some properties were not registered.

maths-2014-ol-p2-q8-a-iv.description: A wind turbine, used to generate electricity, has three equally spaced blades 65 metres long. The expected lifetime of the turbine is 25 years. On average, the turbine operates 31% of the time. The blades rotate 15 times per minute when the turbine is operating. Find the number of times the blades will rotate during the expected lifetime of the turbine (ignore leap years). Write your answer in the form a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n ∈ ℤ.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q1-a.description: z = 4/(1 + √3i) is a complex number, where i² = −1. Verify that z can be written as 1 − √3i.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q1-b.description: z = 4/(1 + √3i) is a complex number, where i² = −1. Plot z on an Argand diagram and write z in polar form.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q1-c.description: z = 4/(1 + √3i) is a complex number, where i² = −1. Use De Moivre’s theorem to show that z¹⁰ = −2⁹(1 − √3i).

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q2-a.description: Find the set of all real values of x for which 2x² + x − 15 ≥ 0.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q2-b.description: Solve the simultaneous equations: x + y + z = 16; (5/2)x + y + 10z = 40; 2x + (1/2)y + 4z = 21.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q3-a.description: Scientists can estimate the age of certain ancient items by measuring the proportion of carbon–14, relative to the total carbon content in the item. The formula used is Q = e^(−0·693t/5730), where Q is the proportion of carbon–14 remaining and t is the age, in years, of the item. An item is 2000 years old. Use the formula to find the proportion of carbon–14 in the item.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q3-b.description: Scientists can estimate the age of certain ancient items by measuring the proportion of carbon–14, relative to the total carbon content in the item. The formula used is Q = e^(−0·693t/5730), where Q is the proportion of carbon–14 remaining and t is the age, in years, of the item. The proportion of carbon–14 in an item found at Lough Boora, County Offaly, was 0·3402. Estimate, correct to two significant figures, the age of the item.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q4-a-i.description: Niamh has saved to buy a car. She saved an equal amount at the beginning of each month in an account that earned an annual equivalent rate (AER) of 4%. Show that the rate of interest, compounded monthly, which is equivalent to an AER of 4% is 0·327%, correct to 3 decimal places.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q4-a-ii.description: Niamh has saved to buy a car. She saved an equal amount at the beginning of each month in an account that earned an annual equivalent rate (AER) of 4%. Part (a)(i): the equivalent monthly interest rate is 0·327%, correct to 3 decimal places. Niamh has €15 000 in the account at the end of 36 months. How much has she saved each month, correct to the nearest euro?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q4-b.description: Conall borrowed to buy a car. He borrowed €15 000 at a monthly interest rate of 0·866%. He made 36 equal monthly payments to repay the entire loan. How much, to the nearest euro, was each of his monthly payments?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q5-a.description: Each diagram shows part of the graph of a function: f, g, h and k. Diagrams A–D show their first derivatives, and I–IV their second derivatives, not necessarily in the same order. Refer to all twelve original graphs. Diagrams A–D show their first derivatives, and I–IV their second derivatives, not necessarily in the same order. Refer to all twelve original graphs. Part (a): match each of the four function types to its function, first derivative and second derivative. For one row in the table, explain your choice of first derivative and second derivative.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q6-a.description: The diagram shows the graph of the function y = sin x in the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ π, x ∈ ℝ. The table lists x = 0, π/6, π/3, π/2, 2π/3, 5π/6, π, with y values left blank. Complete the table below, correct to three decimal places.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q6-b.description: The diagram shows the graph of the function y = sin x in the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ π, x ∈ ℝ. maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q6-c.description: The diagram shows the graph of the function y = sin x in the domain 0 ≤ x ≤ π, x ∈ ℝ. The table lists x = 0, π/6, π/3, π/2, 2π/3, 5π/6, π, with y values left blank. Use integration to find the actual area of the region shown above.

Find the percentage error in your answer to (b) above.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-a.description: A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. If the ticket price was €18, how many people would be expected to attend?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-b.description: A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. Let x be the ticket price, where x ≤ 20. Write down, in terms of x, the expected attendance at such an event.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-c.description: A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. Let x be the ticket price, where x ≤ 20. Write down a function f that gives the expected income from the sale of tickets for such an event.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-d.description: A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. Find the price at which tickets should be sold to give the maximum expected income.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-e.description: A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. Part (d): find the ticket price that maximises expected income. Find this maximum expected income.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-f.description: A stadium can hold 25 000 people. People attending a regular event at the stadium must purchase a ticket in advance. When the ticket price is €20, the expected attendance at an event is 12 000 people. The results of a survey carried out by the owners suggest that for every €1 reduction, from €20, in the ticket price, the expected attendance would increase by 1000 people. Suppose that tickets are instead priced at a value that is expected to give a full attendance at the stadium. Find the difference between the income from the sale of tickets at this price and the maximum income calculated at (e) above.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q7-g.description: The stadium can hold 25 000 people. The stadium was full for a recent special event. Two types of tickets were sold, a single ticket for €16 and a family ticket (2 adults and 2 children) for a certain amount. The income from this event was €365 000. If 1000 more family tickets had been sold, the income from the event would have been reduced by €14 000. How many family tickets were sold?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q8-a.description: The speed at which a raindrop falls increases until a maximum speed, called its terminal velocity, is reached. The raindrop then continues to fall at this terminal velocity. The distance, s metres, it falls is given by s(t) = 6t + 0·3t² − 0·01t³ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, and k(t − 10) for t > 10, as printed. Here t is the time in seconds from the instant the raindrop begins to fall and k is a constant. How far has this raindrop fallen after 10 seconds?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q8-b.description: The speed at which a raindrop falls increases until a maximum speed, called its terminal velocity, is reached. The raindrop then continues to fall at this terminal velocity. The distance, s metres, it falls is given by s(t) = 6t + 0·3t² − 0·01t³ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, and k(t − 10) for t > 10, as printed. Here t is the time in seconds from the instant the raindrop begins to fall and k is a constant. After how many seconds is the raindrop falling at a speed of 8·25 metres per second?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q8-c.description: The speed at which a raindrop falls increases until a maximum speed, called its terminal velocity, is reached. The raindrop then continues to fall at this terminal velocity. The distance, s metres, it falls is given by s(t) = 6t + 0·3t² − 0·01t³ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, and k(t − 10) for t > 10, as printed. Here t is the time in seconds from the instant the raindrop begins to fall and k is a constant. The acceleration of the raindrop is decreasing for the first 10 seconds of its fall. Find the value of t for which the acceleration is 0·006 m s⁻².

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q8-d.description: The speed at which a raindrop falls increases until a maximum speed, called its terminal velocity, is reached. The raindrop then continues to fall at this terminal velocity. The distance, s metres, it falls is given by s(t) = 6t + 0·3t² − 0·01t³ for 0 ≤ t ≤ 10, and k(t − 10) for t > 10, as printed. Here t is the time in seconds from the instant the raindrop begins to fall and k is a constant. The raindrop falls vertically from a height of 620 metres. How long will it take the raindrop to fall to ground level?

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q8-e.description: A raindrop increases in size as it falls. The volume of a spherical raindrop increases at a rate of 6 cubic millimetres per second. Find the rate at which the radius of the raindrop is increasing when the radius is 1·5 mm.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q9-a-i.description: Shapes in the form of small equilateral triangles can be made using matchsticks of equal length. These shapes can be put together into patterns. The first three triangular patterns are shown in the original diagrams. The table for patterns 1–4 gives numbers of small triangles: 1, blank, 9, blank; and numbers of matchsticks: 3, 9, blank, blank. Draw the fourth pattern in the sequence.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q9-d.description: Shapes in the form of small equilateral triangles can be made using matchsticks of equal length. These shapes can be put together into patterns. The first three triangular patterns are shown in the original diagrams. The number of matchsticks in the nth pattern in the sequence can be represented by the function uₙ = an² + bn where a, b ∈ ℚ and n ∈ ℕ. Find the value of a and the value of b.

maths-2013-hl-p1-project-q9-e.description: Shapes in the form of small equilateral triangles can be made using matchsticks of equal length. These shapes can be put together into patterns. The first three triangular patterns are shown in the original diagrams. maths-2013-hl-p2-project-q2-a-ii.description: A random variable X follows a normal distribution with mean 60 and standard deviation 5. Find P(52 ≤ X ≤ 68).

Sketch, on each diagram, a new distribution to show the effect of the hormone. A: increases the height of all plants. B: reduces the number of really small and really tall plants, with the mean unchanged. C: increases the number of small and tall plants, with the mean unchanged.

maths-2013-hl-p2-project-q3-a.description: The equations of six lines are given: h: x = 3 − y; i: 2x − 4y = 3; k: y = −¼(2x − 7); l: 4x − 2y − 5 = 0; m: x + √3y − 10 = 0; n: √3x + y − 10 = 0. At the same time, the water in B is 10 cm deep and its depth increases steadily by 7·5 cm every 10 seconds. Draw up a table showing the depth of water in each tank at 10 second intervals over two minutes, beginning at the time mentioned above.

At a particular time, the water in A is 25 cm deep and its depth increases steadily by 5 cm every 10 seconds. Find, from your graphs, how much time passes before the depth of water is the same in each tank.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q2-b.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Prove that the circles are touching.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q2-c.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Verify that (4, 7) is the point that they have in common.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q2-d.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Part (c): verify that (4, 7) is their point in common. Find the equation of the common tangent.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q3.description: The circle shown has as tangents the x-axis, the y-axis, the line x + y = 2 and the line x + y = 2k, where k > 1. Find k.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q4-a.description: A basketball player scores 60% of the free-throw shots she attempts. During a particular game she gets six free throws. What assumption(s) must be made in order to regard this as a sequence of Bernoulli trials?

maths-2012-hl-p2-q4-b-i.description: A basketball player scores 60% of the free-throw shots she attempts. During a particular game she gets six free throws. Based on the Bernoulli-trial assumptions, find, correct to three decimal places, the probability that she scores on exactly four of the six shots.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q4-b-ii.description: A basketball player scores 60% of the free-throw shots she attempts. During a particular game she gets six free throws. Based on the Bernoulli-trial assumptions, find, correct to three decimal places, the probability that she scores for the second time on the fifth shot.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q5-a.description: A company produces calculator batteries. The diameter is supposed to be 20 mm with tolerance 0·25 mm; batteries outside this tolerance are rejected, and this is the only reason for rejection. A machine produces normally distributed battery diameters with mean 20 mm and standard deviation 0·1 mm. Out of every 10 000 batteries, how many on average are rejected?

maths-2012-hl-p2-q5-b.description: A company produces calculator batteries. The diameter is supposed to be 20 mm with tolerance 0·25 mm; batteries outside this tolerance are rejected, and this is the only reason for rejection. The original diameters were normally distributed with mean 20 mm and standard deviation 0·1 mm. A machine setting slips and the mean diameter increases to 20·05 mm, with standard deviation unchanged. Find the percentage increase in the rejection rate.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q6a-a-i.description: Given the points B and C, construct, without using a protractor or setsquare, a point A such that |∠ABC| = 60°.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q6a-a-ii.description: Part (a)(i): construct A from the supplied B and C so that |∠ABC| = 60°, without a protractor or setsquare. Hence construct, on the same diagram, and using a compass and straight edge only, an angle of 15°.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q6a-b.description: The parallel lines l₁, l₂, l₃ and l₄ make equal intercepts on transversal k. FG is parallel to k, and HG is parallel to ED. Use the original diagram. Prove that triangles CDE and FGH are congruent.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q6b.description: The incircle of triangle ABC has centre O and touches the sides at P, Q and R, as shown. Prove that |∠PQR| = ½(|∠CAB| + |∠CBA|).

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-a-i.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What can you say about the change from September 2009 to September 2011 with regard to the arrears rates?

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-a-ii.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What can you say about the change from September 2009 to September 2011 with regard to the rates of interest being paid?

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-a-iii.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What can you say about the change from September 2009 to September 2011 with regard to the relationship between the arrears rate and the interest rate?

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-b.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What additional information would you need before you could estimate the median interest rate being paid by mortgage holders in September 2011?

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-c.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. The report says “The direction of causality … is important” regarding the September 2011 relationship. Explain what “direction of causality” means in this context.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-d-i.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Find the probability that a property selected at random from all those examined will be in negative equity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-d-ii.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Find the probability that a property selected at random from those in negative equity will also be in arrears. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-d-iii.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Find the probability that a property selected at random from those in arrears will also be in negative equity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q7-e.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Treat the December 2010 study as the population. In early 2012, 552 of 2000 randomly selected mortgaged properties are in negative equity. Use a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to decide whether there is sufficient evidence that the proportion has changed. State the null hypothesis and conclusion clearly.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q8-a.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Determine α and β to locate R 24 cm to the right of P and 7 cm higher. Give the angles correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q8-b.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Part (a) puts R 24 cm right and 7 cm above P. In the position from part (a), which causes the greater error in R’s location: a 1° error in α or in β? Justify your answer. For motion through a small angle, assume distance from the starting point equals the arc length travelled.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q8-c.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Part (b) compares the location errors caused by a 1° error in each angle; for a small angle, the movement is approximately the arc length. The answer to part (b) depends on the position of the arm. Describe, with justification, when R’s location is more sensitive to small errors in α than in β, and when the reverse is true.

maths-2012-hl-p2-q8-d.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Illustrate all possible locations of R on the coordinate diagram. Take P as the origin and each unit as one centimetre in reality. Both α and β can vary only from 0° to 180°.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q1-a.description: When Katie had travelled 140 km, she had completed 4/9 of her journey. Find the length of her journey.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q1-b-i.description: Robert’s electricity bill: day readings 35 087 and 34 537 at €0.1506 per unit; night readings 17 213 and 16 853 at €0.0745 per unit. Calculate the total cost of the units used.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q1-b-ii.description: Robert’s electricity bill: day readings 35 087 and 34 537 at €0.1506 per unit; night readings 17 213 and 16 853 at €0.0745 per unit. Robert also pays a standing charge of €24.89 and a levy of €5.46. VAT at 13.5% is charged on all amounts. Calculate his total electricity bill.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q1-c-i.description: A retailer bought 40 toys at €24.75 each. He sold 10 at €33.88 each and the remaining 30 at a reduced price. Total sales were €1270. Write his total profit as a percentage of his cost, correct to one decimal place.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q1-c-ii.description: A retailer bought 40 toys at €24.75 each. He sold 10 at €33.88 each and the remaining 30 at a reduced price. Total sales were €1270. Find the reduced selling price of each of the remaining 30 toys.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q2-a.description: Solve x − y = 4 and 2x + y = 5 for x and y.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q2-b-i.description: f(x) = x³ + 2x² − x − 2. Show, by division, that x − 1 is a factor of f(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q2-b-ii.description: f(x) = x³ + 2x² − x − 2. Part (i) asks for division by x − 1. Hence, or otherwise, find the other factors of f(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q2-c-i.description: g(x) = 1/x² − 1/(2x) and h(x) = 1 − 2/x, where x ≠ 0 and x is real. Show that h(x) = −2x[g(x)].

maths-2012-ol-p1-q2-c-ii.description: g(x) = 1/x² − 1/(2x) and h(x) = 1 − 2/x, where x ≠ 0 and x is real. Find the values of x for which g(x) = h(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q3-b-i.description: x − y + 5 = 0 and x² + y² = 17. Solve for x and y.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q3-b-ii.description: x − y + 5 = 0 and x² + y² = 17. Part (i) asks for both solutions. Which solution gives the lesser value of x − 2y? Write down this value.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q3-c-i.description: Simplify (√x − 2/√x)(√x + 2/√x), where x > 0 and x is real.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q3-c-ii.description: Part (i) asks you to simplify (√x − 2/√x)(√x + 2/√x), where x > 0 and x is real. Hence solve (√x − 2/√x)(√x + 2/√x) = 3, where x > 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q3-c-iii.description: The equation is (√x − 2/√x)(√x + 2/√x) = 3 with x > 0; part (ii) asks for its solution. Verify your solution.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q4-a-i.description: 6 − 4i + 3u = 5i, where i² = −1. Find the value of u.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q4-a-ii.description: 6 − 4i + 3u = 5i, where i² = −1. Part (i) asks for u. Plot u on an Argand diagram.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q4-b-ii.description: z = 1 + i. Show that z² + (conjugate of z)² = 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q4-c.description: Let w = 3 + 4i. Find real k and t such that w² − (k + t)w + t = 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q5-a.description: The nth term of a sequence is Tₙ = (2n − 1)/(n + 1). Find the sum of its second and third terms.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q5-b-i.description: The first term of an arithmetic series is 2 and the eighth term is 30. Find T₃, the third term.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q5-b-ii.description: The first term of an arithmetic series is 2 and the eighth term is 30. Find S₁₀, the sum of the first ten terms.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q5-c-i.description: The nth term of a series is Tₙ = 2/(3^(n + 1)). Write an expression in n for Tₙ₋₁, the (n − 1)st term.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q5-c-ii.description: The nth term of a series is Tₙ = 2/(3^(n + 1)). Part (i) asks for Tₙ₋₁. Prove the series is geometric.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q5-c-iii.description: The nth term of a series is Tₙ = 2/(3^(n + 1)). Show S₉ = 1/3 − 1/3¹⁰, where S₉ is the sum of the first nine terms.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-a.description: Let h(x) = ax + b for real x. Given h(0) = 3 and h(2) = −5, find a and b.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-b-i.description: The original diagram shows part of the graph of a function f. Use the graph to estimate the values of x for which f(x) = 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-b-ii.description: The original diagram shows part of the graph of a function f. Use the graph to estimate the values of x for which f′(x) = 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-b-iii.description: The original diagram shows part of the graph of a function f. Part (ii) asks where f′(x) = 0. Use the graph to estimate the range of x for which f′(x) < 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-c-i.description: g(x) = x(3x² − 9), where x is real. Find g′(x), the derivative of g(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-c-ii.description: g(x) = x(3x² − 9), where x is real. Find the coordinates of the local maximum and local minimum of y = g(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q6-c-iii.description: g(x) = x(3x² − 9), where x is real. Part (i) asks for g′(x). Draw g′(x), the derivative of g(x), for −2 ≤ x ≤ 2.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q7-a.description: Differentiate y = 6x − x² − 5x⁴ with respect to x.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q7-b-i.description: Differentiate y = (3x² + 2)(x³ − x) with respect to x.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q7-b-ii.description: Given y = (x³ − 2x² + 4)⁵, find dy/dx at x = −1.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q7-c-i.description: A ball is thrown vertically down from the top of a high building. The distance it falls is s = 3t + 5t² metres, where t is seconds from release. Find its speed after 3 seconds.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q7-c-ii.description: A ball is thrown vertically down from the top of a high building. The distance it falls is s = 3t + 5t² metres, where t is seconds from release. Find t when the speed is 23 m s⁻¹.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q7-c-iii.description: A ball is thrown vertically down from the top of a high building. The distance it falls is s = 3t + 5t² metres, where t is seconds from release. The ball hits the ground at 38 m s⁻¹. How high is the building?

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-a.description: Let g(x) = k(1 − x) for real x. Given g(−5) = 20, find k.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-b-i.description: f(x) = (5 + x²)/(2 − x), where x is real and x ≠ 2. Find f(5).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-b-ii.description: f(x) = (5 + x²)/(2 − x), where x is real and x ≠ 2. Find f′(x), the derivative of f(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-b-iii.description: f(x) = (5 + x²)/(2 − x), where x is real and x ≠ 2. Part (ii) asks for f′(x). Show f′(x) = 0 at x = −1.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-c-i.description: h(x) = 5 + 3x − x², where x is real. Find the coordinates of P where y = h(x) cuts the y-axis.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-c-ii.description: h(x) = 5 + 3x − x², where x is real. P is the y-intercept found in part (i). Find the equation of the tangent to y = h(x) at P.

maths-2012-ol-p1-q8-c-iii.description: h(x) = 5 + 3x − x², where x is real. P is the y-intercept; part (ii) asks for the tangent at P. The tangent at x = t is perpendicular to the tangent at P. Find t.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q1-a.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. Write out the sample space showing all the possible outcomes. For example, BGG is one outcome, representing Boy, Girl, Girl.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q1-b.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. Peter says these outcomes are equally likely. Niamh says they are not. What do you need to know about the students in the school to decide which of them is correct?

maths-2012-ol-p2-q1-c.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. If all the outcomes are equally likely, what is the probability that the three students will be two girls followed by a boy?

maths-2012-ol-p2-q1-d.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. Niamh guesses there will be at least one girl; Peter guesses there will be either three boys or two boys and a girl. Who is more likely to be correct, assuming all outcomes are equally likely? Justify your answer.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q2-a.description: The universal set is a normal deck of 52 playing cards. The two sets represent clubs and picture cards (kings, queens and jacks). Show on the Venn diagram the number of elements in each region.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q2-b-i.description: A card is drawn from a pack of 52 cards. Find the probability that the card drawn is the king of clubs.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q2-b-ii.description: Picture cards are kings, queens and jacks. A card is drawn from a pack of 52 cards. Find the probability that the card drawn is a club or a picture card.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q2-b-iii.description: Picture cards are kings, queens and jacks. Two cards are drawn from a pack of 52 cards. Find the probability that neither is a club or a picture card. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q3-a.description: A(6, −1), B(12, −3), C(8, 5) and D(2, 7) are four points. Plot the four points on the diagram below.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q3-b.description: A(6, −1), B(12, −3), C(8, 5) and D(2, 7) are four points. Describe two different ways of showing, using co-ordinate geometry techniques, that the points form a parallelogram ABCD.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q3-c.description: A(6, −1), B(12, −3), C(8, 5) and D(2, 7) are four points. Part (b) asks for two different co-ordinate geometry methods. Use one of the ways you have described to show that ABCD is a parallelogram.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q4-a.description: Two circles c₁ and c₂ have equal radius. c₁ has centre (0, 0) and cuts the x-axis at (5, 0). Use the original diagram. Find the equation of c₁.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q4-b.description: Two circles c₁ and c₂ have equal radius. c₁ has centre (0, 0) and cuts the x-axis at (5, 0). Use the original diagram. Show that the point P(−3, 4) is on c₁.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q4-c.description: Two circles c₁ and c₂ have equal radius. c₁ has centre (0, 0) and cuts the x-axis at (5, 0). Use the original diagram. The two circles touch at P(−3, 4). P is on the line joining the two centres. Find the equation of c₂.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q4-d.description: Two circles c₁ and c₂ have equal radius. c₁ has centre (0, 0) and cuts the x-axis at (5, 0). Use the original diagram. The circles touch at P(−3, 4), which lies on the line joining their centres. Find the equation of the common tangent at P.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q5a-a-i.description: Write down a geometrical result that can be used to construct a tangent to a circle at a point.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q5a-a-ii.description: On the diagram shown, construct the tangent to the circle at A.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q5a-b.description: Construct the circumcentre and circumcircle of the triangle below, using only a straight edge and compass. Show all construction marks clearly.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q5b.description: ABCD is a parallelogram. A, B and C lie on the circle which cuts [AD] at P. The line CP meets BA at Q. Prove that |CD| = |CP|.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-a-i.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Show the annual total sales of cars over the six years, using a suitable chart.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-a-ii.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Find the mean number of cars sold per year over the six years.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-a-iii.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Calculate the percentage increase in annual car sales between 2009 and 2011.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-a-iv.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Part (a)(iii) calculates the increase from 2009 to 2011. Aoife says the increase shows car sales are currently going well. Paul says they are going badly: sales have fallen by 52% since 2007 and are well below average. Complete the sentences to give a criticism of each argument.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-a-v.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Give a more balanced description of the pattern of car sales over the six years.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-b-i.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Describe how the sales of the cars are distributed over the four quarters of each year.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-b-ii.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Part (b)(i) describes the distribution over the four quarters. Suggest a reason for this pattern of sales.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-b-iii.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. The sales for the first quarter of 2012 are 36 081. Find, with justification, an estimate for the total annual sales for 2012.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-c-i.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Two pie charts show the change from 2006 to 2011 in the popularity of petrol and diesel cars. Complete the second pie chart.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-c-ii.description: Use the original table of new private cars sold in Ireland in each quarter of each year from 2006 to 2011, including the annual totals and engine types. Which of statements A–E best describes the change over time in the popularity of diesel cars as a percentage of the total? Write the letter corresponding to the correct answer in the box.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-d-i.description: Use the original CO₂ emissions data (g/km) for the 12 diesel and 12 petrol models. Part (d)(i) asks for a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot. Construct a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot of the above data.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-d-ii.description: Use the original CO₂ emissions data (g/km) for the 12 diesel and 12 petrol models. Part (d)(i) asks for a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot. Does the information suggest that diesel engines produce lower CO₂ emissions than petrol engines? Refer to the stem-and-leaf plot and an appropriate measure of central tendency.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q6-d-iii.description: Use the original CO₂ emissions data (g/km) for the 12 diesel and 12 petrol models. Part (d)(i) asks for a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot. Does the information suggest greater variation in the CO₂ emissions of diesel engines than petrol engines? Refer to the stem-and-leaf plot and an appropriate measure of variability.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q7-a.description: The planned roof supports form scalene triangles of different sizes. Explain what is meant by a scalene triangle.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q7-b.description: Triangles ABC, CDE and EFG form roof supports. CDE is the enlargement of ABC and EFG is the enlargement of CDE under the same enlargement. |AB| = 7·2 m, |BC| = 8 m, |CD| = 9 m and |∠DCB| = 60°. Use the original diagram. Find the length of [FG].

maths-2012-ol-p2-q7-c.description: Triangles ABC, CDE and EFG form roof supports. CDE is the enlargement of ABC and EFG is the enlargement of CDE under the same enlargement. |AB| = 7·2 m, |BC| = 8 m, |CD| = 9 m and |∠DCB| = 60°. Use the original diagram. Find the length of [BD], correct to three decimal places.

maths-2012-ol-p2-q7-d.description: Triangles ABC, CDE and EFG form roof supports. CDE is the enlargement of ABC and EFG is the enlargement of CDE under the same enlargement. |AB| = 7·2 m, |BC| = 8 m, |CD| = 9 m and |∠DCB| = 60°. Use the original diagram. The centre of the enlargement is O. Find the distance from O to the point B.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q8-e.description: A company makes conical drinking cups from a sector AOB cut from a circular piece of waterproof paper of radius 9 cm. Edges AO and OB are joined. The rim radius is r and the cup height is h. Refer to the original sector and cup diagrams. The capacity is V = (π/3)h(81 − h²) cm³. Compare the two cups with capacity 154π/3 and the cup of maximum volume; calculate their radii and heights as in parts (b)–(d). In practice, which one of the three cups above is the most reasonable shape for a conical cup? Give a reason for your answer.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q8-f.description: A company makes conical drinking cups from a sector AOB cut from a circular piece of waterproof paper of radius 9 cm. Edges AO and OB are joined. The rim radius is r and the cup height is h. Refer to the original sector and cup diagrams. The capacity is V = (π/3)h(81 − h²) cm³. Parts (b)–(e): compare the two cups with capacity 154π/3 and the maximum-volume cup; select and justify the most reasonable cup. For the cup you have chosen in part (e), find the measure of the angle AOB that must be cut from the circular disc in order to make the cup. Give your answer in degrees, correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-a-i.description: Atmospheric pressure is measured in kilopascals (kPa) and decreases with altitude. The supplied data gives altitudes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km and respective pressures 101·3, 89·9, 79·5, 70·1, 61·6, 54·0 kPa. Hannah models the data as a geometric sequence with first term 101·3 and common ratio 0·883. Complete the table to show the values given by Hannah’s model, correct to one decimal place.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-a-ii.description: Atmospheric pressure is measured in kilopascals (kPa) and decreases with altitude. The supplied data gives altitudes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km and respective pressures 101·3, 89·9, 79·5, 70·1, 61·6, 54·0 kPa. Hannah models the data as a geometric sequence with first term 101·3 and common ratio 0·883. First calculate the model values for altitudes 1–5 km, to one decimal place. By considering the percentage errors in the above values, insert an appropriate number to complete: “Hannah’s model is accurate to within ________%.”

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-b-i-altitude.description: Atmospheric pressure is measured in kilopascals (kPa) and decreases with altitude. The supplied data gives altitudes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km and respective pressures 101·3, 89·9, 79·5, 70·1, 61·6, 54·0 kPa. Hannah models the data as a geometric sequence with first term 101·3 and common ratio 0·883. Thomas models pressure using p = 101·3e^(−0·1244h), where p is in kPa and h is altitude in km. Taking any one value other than 0 for the altitude, verify that the pressure given by Thomas’s model and the pressure given by Hannah’s model differ by less than 0·01 kPa.

Atmospheric pressure is measured in kilopascals (kPa) and decreases with altitude. The supplied data gives altitudes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km and respective pressures 101·3, 89·9, 79·5, 70·1, 61·6, 54·0 kPa. maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-b-ii.description: Atmospheric pressure is measured in kilopascals (kPa) and decreases with altitude. The supplied data gives altitudes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km and respective pressures 101·3, 89·9, 79·5, 70·1, 61·6, 54·0 kPa. Hannah models the data as a geometric sequence with first term 101·3 and common ratio 0·883. Thomas models pressure using p = 101·3e^(−0·1244h), where p is in kPa and h is altitude in km. Explain how Thomas might have arrived at the value of the constant 0·1244 in his model.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-c.description: Atmospheric pressure is measured in kilopascals (kPa) and decreases with altitude. The supplied data gives altitudes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km and respective pressures 101·3, 89·9, 79·5, 70·1, 61·6, 54·0 kPa. Hannah models the data as a geometric sequence with first term 101·3 and common ratio 0·883. Thomas models pressure using p = 101·3e^(−0·1244h), where p is in kPa and h is altitude in km. Hannah’s model is discrete, while Thomas’s is continuous. (i) Explain what this means. (ii) State one advantage of a continuous model over a discrete one.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-d.description: Thomas models pressure using p = 101·3e^(−0·1244h), where p is in kPa and h is altitude in km. Use Thomas’s model to estimate the atmospheric pressure at the altitude of the top of Mount Everest: 8848 metres.

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-e.description: Thomas models pressure using p = 101·3e^(−0·1244h), where p is in kPa and h is altitude in km. Using Thomas’s model, find an estimate for the altitude at which the atmospheric pressure is half of its value at sea level (altitude 0 km).

maths-2012-hl-p1-project-q9-f.description: Thomas models pressure using p = 101·3e^(−0·1244h), where p is in kPa and h is altitude in km. People sometimes experience a sensation in their ears when pressure changes rapidly by 1 kilopascal or more. Suppose such a person steps into a fast lift close to sea level. Taking a suitable approximation for the distance between two floors, estimate the number of floors the person would need to travel to feel this sensation.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q1-a.description: Given the co-ordinates of the vertices of a quadrilateral ABCD, describe three different ways to determine, using co-ordinate geometry techniques, whether the quadrilateral is a parallelogram.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q1-b.description: Part (a): describe three different co-ordinate geometry methods for deciding whether a quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Using one of the methods you described, determine whether the quadrilateral with vertices (−4, −2), (21, −5), (8, 7) and (−17, 10) is a parallelogram.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q2-a.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Write down the centre and radius-length of each circle.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q2-b.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Prove that the circles are touching.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q2-c.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Verify that (4, 7) is the point that they have in common.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q2-d.description: c₁: x² + y² − 6x − 10y + 29 = 0; c₂: x² + y² − 2x − 2y − 43 = 0. Part (c): verify that (4, 7) is their point in common. Find the equation of the common tangent.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q3.description: The circle shown has as tangents the x-axis, the y-axis, the line x + y = 2 and the line x + y = 2k, where k > 1. Find k.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q4-a.description: A basketball player scores 60% of the free-throw shots she attempts. During a particular game she gets six free throws. What assumption(s) must be made in order to regard this as a sequence of Bernoulli trials?

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q4-b-i.description: A basketball player scores 60% of the free-throw shots she attempts. During a particular game she gets six free throws. Based on the Bernoulli-trial assumptions, find, correct to three decimal places, the probability that she scores on exactly four of the six shots.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q4-b-ii.description: A basketball player scores 60% of the free-throw shots she attempts. During a particular game she gets six free throws. Based on the Bernoulli-trial assumptions, find, correct to three decimal places, the probability that she scores for the second time on the fifth shot.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q5-a.description: A company produces calculator batteries. The diameter is supposed to be 20 mm with tolerance 0·25 mm; batteries outside this tolerance are rejected, and this is the only reason for rejection. A machine produces normally distributed battery diameters with mean 20 mm and standard deviation 0·1 mm. Out of every 10 000 batteries, how many on average are rejected?

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q5-b.description: A company produces calculator batteries. The diameter is supposed to be 20 mm with tolerance 0·25 mm; batteries outside this tolerance are rejected, and this is the only reason for rejection. The original diameters were normally distributed with mean 20 mm and standard deviation 0·1 mm. A machine setting slips and the mean diameter increases to 20·05 mm, with standard deviation unchanged. Find the percentage increase in the rejection rate.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q6a-a-i.description: Given the points B and C, construct, without using a protractor or setsquare, a point A such that |∠ABC| = 60°.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q6a-a-ii.description: Part (a)(i): construct A from the supplied B and C so that |∠ABC| = 60°, without a protractor or setsquare. Hence construct, on the same diagram, and using a compass and straight edge only, an angle of 15°.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q6a-b.description: The parallel lines l₁, l₂, l₃ and l₄ make equal intercepts on transversal k. FG is parallel to k, and HG is parallel to ED. Use the original diagram. Prove that triangles CDE and FGH are congruent.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q6b.description: The incircle of triangle ABC has centre O and touches the sides at P, Q and R, as shown. Prove that |∠PQR| = ½(|∠CAB| + |∠CBA|).

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-a-i.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What can you say about the change from September 2009 to September 2011 with regard to the arrears rates?

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-a-ii.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What can you say about the change from September 2009 to September 2011 with regard to the rates of interest being paid?

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-a-iii.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What can you say about the change from September 2009 to September 2011 with regard to the relationship between the arrears rate and the interest rate?

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-b.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. What additional information would you need before you could estimate the median interest rate being paid by mortgage holders in September 2011?

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-c.description: In arrears means a mortgage repayment is overdue by 90 days or more. The two original charts compare September 2009 and September 2011. Each dot represents a group paying a particular interest rate to a lender; the arrears rate is the percentage in arrears. Pay attention to the different axis scales. The report says “The direction of causality … is important” regarding the September 2011 relationship. Explain what “direction of causality” means in this context.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-d-i.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Find the probability that a property selected at random from all those examined will be in negative equity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-d-ii.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Find the probability that a property selected at random from those in negative equity will also be in arrears. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-d-iii.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Find the probability that a property selected at random from those in arrears will also be in negative equity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q7-e.description: A property is in negative equity when its mortgage debt exceeds its value. In December 2010, 475 136 mortgaged properties were examined: 145 414 were in negative equity; 11 644 of those were also in arrears; 317 355 were in neither arrears nor negative equity. In arrears means 90 days or more. Treat the December 2010 study as the population. In early 2012, 552 of 2000 randomly selected mortgaged properties are in negative equity. Use a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to decide whether there is sufficient evidence that the proportion has changed. State the null hypothesis and conclusion clearly.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q8-a.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Determine α and β to locate R 24 cm to the right of P and 7 cm higher. Give the angles correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q8-b.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Part (a) puts R 24 cm right and 7 cm above P. In the position from part (a), which causes the greater error in R’s location: a 1° error in α or in β? Justify your answer. For motion through a small angle, assume distance from the starting point equals the arc length travelled.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q8-c.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Part (b) compares the location errors caused by a 1° error in each angle; for a small angle, the movement is approximately the arc length. The answer to part (b) depends on the position of the arm. Describe, with justification, when R’s location is more sensitive to small errors in α than in β, and when the reverse is true.

maths-2012-hl-p2-project-q8-d.description: The robotic arm moves in a vertical plane. P and the segment lengths are fixed; α and β each vary from 0° to 180°. |PQ| = 20 cm and |QR| = 12 cm. Use the original labelled diagram. Illustrate all possible locations of R on the coordinate diagram. Take P as the origin and each unit as one centimetre in reality. Both α and β can vary only from 0° to 180°.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q1-a.description: Alan pays income tax, USC and PRSI on gross weekly wages of €510. Alan pays income tax at 20% and has weekly tax credits of €63. How much income tax does he pay?

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q1-b.description: Alan pays income tax, USC and PRSI on gross weekly wages of €510. Alan pays USC at 2% on the first €193, 4% on the next €115 and 7% on the balance. Calculate the amount of USC he pays.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q1-c.description: Alan pays income tax, USC and PRSI on gross weekly wages of €510. Income tax is 20%, with €63 weekly credits. USC is 2% on €193, 4% on the next €115, then 7% on the balance. His total weekly deductions are €76·92. How much PRSI does Alan pay?

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q2-a.description: Let a = √2. For each number a, a − 1, (−a)², (a − 2)² and 1 + a², tick whether it is rational or irrational.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q2-b.description: Let a = √2. Show a, −a, √a and a⁻² on the number line.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q2-c.description: Verify that 3 − √2 is a root of x² − 6x + 7 = 0.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q3-a.description: The complex number z = 1 − 4i, where i² = −1. Plot z and −2z on the Argand diagram.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q3-b-c-d.description: The complex number z = 1 − 4i, where i² = −1. Part (a) asks you to plot z and −2z; use the original Argand diagram. (b) Show that 2|z| = |−2z|. (c) What does this tell you about the points plotted in (a)? (d) Let k be real with |z + k| = 5. Find the two possible values of k.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q4-a-b.description: (a) Solve ½(7x − 2) + 5 = 2x + 7. (b) Solve 2/(3x − 4) − 1/(2x + 1) = ½, giving answers to one decimal place.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q5-a.description: Use the original graph of f. The graph of g is a straight line with g(−1) = −6 and g(3) = 6. Draw the graph of g on the diagram.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q5-b.description: Use the original graph of f. The graph of g is a straight line with g(−1) = −6 and g(3) = 6. Use the graphs to find both values of x for which g(x) = f(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q5-c.description: Use the original graph of f. The graph of g is a straight line with g(−1) = −6 and g(3) = 6. For x ∈ ℝ, g(x) = ax + b and f(x) = x² + px + q, where a, b, p, q are constants. The graph of f crosses the x-axis at −1 and 3. Find a, b, p, q and use algebra to solve g(x) = f(x).

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q6-a.description: The original diagram shows f(x) = x³ − x² − x + 6 for x ∈ ℝ. Find the coordinates of the point at which f cuts the y-axis.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q6-b.description: The original diagram shows f(x) = x³ − x² − x + 6 for x ∈ ℝ. f has a minimum turning point at (1, 5). Find the coordinates of the maximum turning point.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q6-c.description: The original diagram shows f(x) = x³ − x² − x + 6 for x ∈ ℝ. The lines k and l are parallel tangents to y = f(x). The equation of k is 4x − y + 9 = 0. Find the x-coordinate of the point where l is tangent to the curve.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-a.description: In the examination model, Clark’s rule is C = (W/68) × A, where C is the child’s dose, A the adult dose and W the child’s weight in kg. The adult dose is 125 mg per day. Calculate the dose for a child weighing 30 kg using Clark’s rule, to the nearest 5 mg.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-b-i.description: Write a formula that exactly matches the supplied description of Young’s rule. State clearly the meaning of any letters used. Divide the child’s age by the child’s age plus 12, then multiply by the usual adult dose.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-b-ii.description: Write a formula that exactly matches the supplied description of Young’s rule. State clearly the meaning of any letters used. Add 12 to the child’s age, divide the sum by the child’s age, then divide the adult dose by the figure obtained.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-b-iii.description: Write a formula that exactly matches the supplied description of Young’s rule. State clearly the meaning of any letters used. Multiply the adult dose by the child’s age in years and divide the result by the child’s age plus 12.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-c.description: Young’s rule is described three ways: divide age by (age + 12), then multiply by adult dose; divide adult dose by ((age + 12)/age); or divide (adult dose × age) by (age + 12). Explain why the three formulae in part (b) all give the same result.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-d.description: Young’s rule is described three ways: divide age by (age + 12), then multiply by adult dose; divide adult dose by ((age + 12)/age); or divide (adult dose × age) by (age + 12). The adult dose is 150 mg per day. According to Young’s rule, what is the correct dose for a six-year-old child?

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-e.description: Young’s rule is described three ways: divide age by (age + 12), then multiply by adult dose; divide adult dose by ((age + 12)/age); or divide (adult dose × age) by (age + 12). Young’s rule gives a child one fifth of the adult dose. How old is the child?

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-f.description: Use the original BSA chart and the examination rule: child’s dose = (child’s BSA in m² / 1·73) × adult dose. Join height on the left scale to weight on the right to read the BSA. The adult dose is 200 mg per day. Use the BSA rule to calculate the dose for a child of height 125 cm and weight 26 kg.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q7-g.description: In the examination model, Clark’s rule is C = (W/68) × A, where C is the child’s dose, A the adult dose and W the child’s weight in kg. Young’s rule is described three ways: divide age by (age + 12), then multiply by adult dose; divide adult dose by ((age + 12)/age); or divide (adult dose × age) by (age + 12). Use the original BSA chart and the examination rule: child’s dose = (child’s BSA in m² / 1·73) × adult dose. Join height on the left scale to weight on the right to read the BSA. A child is nine years old. Clark’s and Young’s rules both give 90 mg per day; the BSA rule gives 130 mg per day. Find the weight and height of the child.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q8-a.description: Lucy arranges 1-cent and 5-cent coins in rows. Use the original row pattern and table. Draw the next row of coins, continuing the same pattern.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q8-b.description: Lucy arranges 1-cent and 5-cent coins in rows. Use the original row pattern and table. Complete the table for rows 4 to 7, giving the number of each denomination, total number and total value.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q8-c.description: Lucy arranges 1-cent and 5-cent coins in rows. Use the original row pattern and table. Complete both sentences in terms of n: (i) if n is odd, row n has ___ 1-cent coins and ___ 5-cent coins; (ii) if n is even, row n has ___ 1-cent coins and ___ 5-cent coins.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q8-d.description: Lucy arranges 1-cent and 5-cent coins in rows. Use the original row pattern and table. Find the total number of coins in the 40th row.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q8-e.description: Lucy arranges 1-cent and 5-cent coins in rows. Use the original row pattern and table. Find the total value of the coins in the 40th row.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q8-f-g.description: Lucy arranges 1-cent and 5-cent coins in rows. Use the original row pattern and table. (f) Which row has coins with a total value of 337 cent? (g) Find the total value of the coins in the first 40 rows.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q9-a-i.description: An investment of €100 is modelled by V = 100 + 45t − 1·5t², where V is its value in euro and t is the number of months since it was made. Find the rate at which its value was changing after 6 months.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q9-a-ii.description: An investment of €100 is modelled by V = 100 + 45t − 1·5t², where V is its value in euro and t is the number of months since it was made. State whether its value was increasing or decreasing after 18 months. Justify your answer.

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q9-a-iii.description: An investment of €100 is modelled by V = 100 + 45t − 1·5t², where V is its value in euro and t is the number of months since it was made. The investment was cashed in at the end of 24 months. How much was it worth then?

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q9-a-iv.description: An investment of €100 is modelled by V = 100 + 45t − 1·5t², where V is its value in euro and t is the number of months since it was made. How much was the investment worth when it had its maximum value?

maths-2012-ol-p1-project-q9-b.description: Garden slabs measure 40 cm by 20 cm, with x slabs on one side and y on the adjacent side of a rectangle. (i) Write the perimeter in cm in terms of x and y. (ii) The perimeter is 64 m; find y in terms of x. (iii) Find x for maximum area. (iv) Find the number of slabs needed.

maths-2012-ol-p2-project-q1-a.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. Write out the sample space showing all the possible outcomes. For example, BGG is one outcome, representing Boy, Girl, Girl.

maths-2012-ol-p2-project-q1-b.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. Peter says these outcomes are equally likely. Niamh says they are not. What do you need to know about the students in the school to decide which of them is correct?

maths-2012-ol-p2-project-q1-c.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl. If all the outcomes are equally likely, what is the probability that the three students will be two girls followed by a boy?

maths-2012-ol-p2-project-q1-d.description: Peter and Niamh arrive early at a large school and guess whether each of the next three students to enter will be a boy or a girl.
