maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q7-b-ii-2.description: A shop sells T-shirts with three sleeve choices (long, short, no sleeve), two neck shapes (round-neck, V-neck), and four colours (white, black, blue, grey). All combinations are available. A customer picks a T-shirt at random from all those available. What is the probability that the customer picks a short-sleeved grey T-shirt?

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q7-b-ii-3.description: A shop sells T-shirts with three sleeve choices (long, short, no sleeve), two neck shapes (round-neck, V-neck), and four colours (white, black, blue, grey). All combinations are available. A customer picks a T-shirt at random from all those available. What is the probability that the customer picks a long-sleeved T-shirt?

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-a-i.description: John hangs two pictures from a horizontal rail. The smaller rectangular frame measures 42 cm by 28 cm. The larger picture is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Use the original diagram. On the diagram, find the centre of enlargement.

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-a-ii.description: John hangs two pictures from a horizontal rail. The smaller rectangular frame measures 42 cm by 28 cm. The larger picture is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Use the original diagram. Find the measurements of the larger picture.

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-a-iii.description: John hangs two pictures from a horizontal rail. The smaller rectangular frame measures 42 cm by 28 cm. The larger picture is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Use the original diagram. The centre of enlargement is 70 cm from the nearest corner of the smaller picture. Find x, the distance between the two pictures.

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-a-iv.description: John hangs two pictures from a horizontal rail. The smaller rectangular frame measures 42 cm by 28 cm. The larger picture is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Use the original diagram. Verify that the ratio of the area of the larger picture to the area of the smaller picture is equal to the square of the scale factor.

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-b-i.description: John moves the larger picture across and up. The original diagram gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 75 cm and vertical side 14 cm. Use Pythagoras’ theorem to find the horizontal length d, correct to the nearest cm.

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-b-ii.description: John moves the larger picture across and up. The original diagram gives a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 75 cm and vertical side 14 cm. Find the angle α between the horizontal and the 75 cm side, correct to the nearest degree.

maths-2012-fl-p2-project-q8-c.description: John hangs two pictures from a horizontal rail. The smaller rectangular frame measures 42 cm by 28 cm. The larger picture is an enlargement with scale factor 2. Use the original diagram. John makes a different frame for the larger picture. Framing material is sold by the metre. He estimates the length needed by calculating the existing perimeter and adding 5%. How many metres of framing material does he need to buy?

maths-2011-hl-p1-q1-b-i.description: Prove the factor theorem for polynomials of degree 2: given f(x) = ax² + bx + c and f(k) = 0, prove that (x − k) is a factor of f(x).

maths-2011-hl-p1-q1-b-ii.description: The factor theorem also holds for polynomials of higher degree. Find the values of n for which (x + k) is a factor of g(x) = xⁿ + kⁿ, where k ≠ 0.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q1-c.description: (x − a)² is a factor of 2x³ − 5ax² + 8abx − 36a, where a ≠ 0. Find the possible values of a and b.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q2-b-i.description: α and 1/α are the roots of 3kx² − 18tx + (2k + 3) = 0, where t and k are constants. Find the value of k.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q2-b-ii.description: α and 1/α are the roots of 3kx² − 18tx + (2k + 3) = 0, where t and k are constants. If one of the roots is four times the other, find the possible values of t.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q2-c-i.description: Let f(x) = 1/(x² − 6x + a), where a is a constant. Prove that if a = 13, then f(x) > 0 for all real x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q2-c-ii.description: Let f(x) = 1/(x² − 6x + a), where a is a constant. Prove that if a = 13, then f(x) < 1 for all real x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q2-c-iii.description: Let f(x) = 1/(x² − 6x + a), where a is a constant. Find the range of values of a such that 0 < f(x) < 1 for all real x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q3-a.description: Express (1 + 2i)/(2 − i) in the form a + bi, where i² = −1.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q3-b-i.description: Find the two complex numbers a + bi such that (a + bi)² = −3 + 4i.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q3-b-ii.description: In part (i), find the two complex numbers a + bi satisfying (a + bi)² = −3 + 4i. Hence solve x² + x + 1 − i = 0.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q3-c-i.description: Let A and B be 2 × 2 matrices, where A has an inverse. Show that (A⁻¹BA)ⁿ = A⁻¹BⁿA for all natural numbers n.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q3-c-ii.description: Let P = [[3, 1], [5, 2]] and M = [[−5, 3], [−10, 6]]. Evaluate P⁻¹MP and hence (P⁻¹MP)ⁿ.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q3-c-iii.description: Let P = [[3, 1], [5, 2]] and M = [[−5, 3], [−10, 6]]. The preceding parts establish (A⁻¹BA)ⁿ = A⁻¹BⁿA and ask you to evaluate P⁻¹MP and its nth power. Hence, or otherwise, show that Mⁿ = M for all natural numbers n.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q4-a.description: In an arithmetic sequence, the third term is −3 and the sixth term is −15. Find the first term and the common difference.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q4-b-i.description: Let uₙ = l(1/2)ⁿ + m(−1)ⁿ for all natural numbers n. Verify that uₙ satisfies 2uₙ₊₂ + uₙ₊₁ − uₙ = 0.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q4-b-ii.description: Let uₙ = l(1/2)ⁿ + m(−1)ⁿ for all natural numbers n. If aₖ = uₖ + uₖ₊₁, express aₖ in terms of k and l.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q4-b-iii.description: Let uₙ = l(1/2)ⁿ + m(−1)ⁿ for all natural numbers n. Define aₖ = uₖ + uₖ₊₁. Find the sum of aₖ from k = 1 to infinity, in terms of l.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q4-b-iv.description: Let uₙ = l(1/2)ⁿ + m(−1)ⁿ for all natural numbers n. Define aₖ = uₖ + uₖ₊₁. For l > 0, find the least positive integer n for which the sum of aₖ from k = 1 to n exceeds 0.99 times its sum from k = 1 to infinity.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q5-a.description: Find the coefficient of x⁸ in the expansion of (x² − 1)¹⁰.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q5-b-ii.description: Solve 3^(2x + 1) − 17(3^x) − 6 = 0. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q5-c.description: Prove by induction that 9 is a factor of 5^(2n + 1) + 2^(4n + 2), for all natural numbers n.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-a.description: Differentiate cos²x with respect to x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-b-i.description: The equation of a curve is y = e^(−x²). Find dy/dx.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-b-ii.description: The equation of a curve is y = e^(−x²). Find the co-ordinates of the turning point of the curve.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-b-iii.description: The equation of a curve is y = e^(−x²). Determine whether this turning point is a local maximum or a local minimum.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-c-i.description: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x + 1), where x is real and x ≠ −1. Find the equations of the asymptotes of y = f(x).

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-c-ii.description: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x + 1), where x is real and x ≠ −1. P and Q are distinct points on y = f(x). The tangent at Q is parallel to the tangent at P, where P = (1, 1). Find the co-ordinates of Q.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q6-c-iii.description: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x + 1), where x is real and x ≠ −1. P = (1, 1), Q is distinct from P, and the tangents at P and Q are parallel. Verify that the intersection of the asymptotes is the midpoint of [PQ].

maths-2011-hl-p1-q7-a.description: Find the slope of the tangent to x² + y³ = x − 2 at (3, −2).

maths-2011-hl-p1-q7-b-i.description: A curve is defined by x = (t − 1)/(t + 1) and y = −4t/(t + 1)², where t ≠ −1. Find dx/dt and dy/dt.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q7-b-ii.description: A curve is defined by x = (t − 1)/(t + 1) and y = −4t/(t + 1)², where t ≠ −1. Hence find dy/dx, and express your answer in terms of x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q7-c-i.description: For real x excluding −1 and 0, f(x) = tan⁻¹(−x/(x + 1)) and g(x) = tan⁻¹((x + 1)/x). Show that f′(x) = −1/(2x² + 2x + 1).

maths-2011-hl-p1-q7-c-ii.description: For real x excluding −1 and 0, f(x) = tan⁻¹(−x/(x + 1)) and g(x) = tan⁻¹((x + 1)/x). The preceding part establishes f′(x) = −1/(2x² + 2x + 1). It can be shown that f′(x) = g′(x). Based only on the derivatives, state which of the three original diagrams A, B or C represents parts of the graphs of f and g, and why each other diagram is incorrect.

maths-2011-hl-p1-q8-c.description: Use integration methods to establish A = πr² for the area of a disc of radius r.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q1-a.description: Find the Cartesian equation of the circle defined by x = 2 + 3 sin θ and y = 3 cos θ, where θ is real.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q1-b.description: Find the equation of the circle through (0, 3), (2, 1) and (6, 5).

maths-2011-hl-p2-q1-c-i.description: c₁: x² + y² − 8x + 2y − 23 = 0 has centre A and radius r₁. c₂: x² + y² + 6x + 4y + 3 = 0 has centre B and radius r₂. Show that c₁ and c₂ intersect at two points.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q1-c-ii.description: c₁: x² + y² − 8x + 2y − 23 = 0 has centre A and radius r₁. c₂: x² + y² + 6x + 4y + 3 = 0 has centre B and radius r₂. Show that the tangents to c₁ at its two intersections with c₂ pass through the centre of c₂.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q2-a.description: Find s and t such that s(i − 4j) + t(2i + 3j) = 4i − 27j.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q2-b-i.description: O is the origin, OP = 3i − 4j, and OQ = 5(OP⊥). Find OQ in terms of i and j.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q2-b-ii.description: O is the origin, OP = 3i − 4j, and OQ = 5(OP⊥). Find cos ∠OQP in surd form.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q2-c-i.description: ABC is a triangle; D is the midpoint of [BC]. Express AB and AC in terms of AD and BC.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q2-c-ii.description: ABC is a triangle; D is the midpoint of [BC]. First express AB and AC in terms of AD and BC. Hence prove |AB|² + |AC|² = 2|AD|² + ½|BC|².

maths-2011-hl-p2-q3-a.description: P = (−1, 4) and Q = (3, 7). Find the point that divides [PQ] internally in the ratio 3 : 1.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q3-b-i.description: f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x − y and y′ = 2x + 3y. The line l₁ is 2x − y − 1 = 0. Find the equation of f(l₁).

maths-2011-hl-p2-q3-b-ii.description: f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x − y and y′ = 2x + 3y. The line l₁ is 2x − y − 1 = 0. Prove that f maps every pair of parallel lines to a pair of parallel lines. You may assume that f maps every line to a line.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q3-b-iii.description: f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x − y and y′ = 2x + 3y. The line l₁ is 2x − y − 1 = 0. O is the origin. The line l₂ is parallel to l₁. Its image meets the x-axis at A′ and the y-axis at B′. If triangle A′OB′ has area 9, find both possible equations of l₂.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q3-b-iv.description: f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x − y and y′ = 2x + 3y. The line l₁ is 2x − y − 1 = 0. The line l₂ is parallel to l₁. Its image meets the axes at A′ and B′, and triangle A′OB′ has area 9. O is the origin. Given A′ = f(A) and B′ = f(B), show that ∠AOB ≠ ∠A′OB′.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q4-a.description: Evaluate the limit as x → 0 of (sin 2x + sin x)/(3x).

maths-2011-hl-p2-q4-b.description: Find all solutions of sin 2x + cos x = 0 for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q4-c-i.description: Two circles are concentric. A tangent to the inner circle cuts the outer circle at B and C, with |BC| = 2x. The shaded region is the annulus shown. Express the area of the shaded region in terms of x.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q4-c-ii.description: Two circles are concentric. A tangent to the inner circle cuts the outer circle at B and C, with |BC| = 2x. The shaded region is the annulus shown. If the outer radius is 2x, show that the portion of the shaded region below BC has area (2π/3 − √3)x².

maths-2011-hl-p2-q5-a.description: Find all values of x satisfying 3 tan x = √3, where 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q5-b-i.description: Prove tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B)/(1 − tan A tan B).

maths-2011-hl-p2-q5-b-ii.description: Show that if α + β = 90°, then tan 2α / tan 2β = −1.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q5-c-i.description: A and B are helicopter landing pads on level ground, and C is on the same level. |BC| = 800 m, |AC| = 900 m, ∠BCA = 60°. A helicopter D is vertically above A; its angle of elevation from C is 30°. Find |AD| in surd form.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q5-c-ii.description: A and B are helicopter landing pads on level ground, and C is on the same level. |BC| = 800 m, |AC| = 900 m, ∠BCA = 60°. A helicopter D is vertically above A; its angle of elevation from C is 30°. Find |BD|.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-a.description: Two adults and four children stand in a row. How many arrangements have all four children between the two adults?

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-b-i.description: uₙ₊₂ − 6uₙ₊₁ + 8uₙ = 0 for n ≥ 0, with u₀ = 0 and u₁ = 4. Solve the difference equation.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-b-ii.description: uₙ₊₂ − 6uₙ₊₁ + 8uₙ = 0 for n ≥ 0, with u₀ = 0 and u₁ = 4. For what value of n is uₙ = 30(2ⁿ)?

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-c-i.description: Five cards are drawn together at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that all five are diamonds, in decimal form correct to two significant figures.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-c-ii.description: Five cards are drawn together at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that all five are of the same suit, in decimal form correct to two significant figures.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-c-iii.description: Five cards are drawn together at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that they are the ace, two, three, four and five of diamonds, in decimal form correct to two significant figures.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q6-c-iv.description: Five cards are drawn together at random from a standard pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability that they include the four aces, in decimal form correct to two significant figures.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-a-i.description: A team of four is selected from seven girls and five boys. How many different selections are possible?

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-a-ii.description: A team of four is selected from seven girls and five boys. How many selections include at least one girl?

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-b-i.description: A marble falls from A along the original triangular network. Every path to the bottom row is equally likely. The rows are A; B,C; D,E,F; G,H,J,K; L,M,N,P,Q. One path from A to H is A–B–D–H. List the other two.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-b-ii.description: A marble falls from A along the original triangular network. Every path to the bottom row is equally likely. The rows are A; B,C; D,E,F; G,H,J,K; L,M,N,P,Q. Find the probability that the marble passes through H or J.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-b-iii.description: A marble falls from A along the original triangular network. Every path to the bottom row is equally likely. The rows are A; B,C; D,E,F; G,H,J,K; L,M,N,P,Q. Find the probability that the marble lands at N.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-b-iv.description: A marble falls from A along the original triangular network. Every path to the bottom row is equally likely. The rows are A; B,C; D,E,F; G,H,J,K; L,M,N,P,Q. Two marbles fall independently from A. Find the probability that both land at P.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-c-i.description: The real numbers a, b and c have mean μ and standard deviation σ. Show that (a − μ)/σ, (b − μ)/σ and (c − μ)/σ have mean 0.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q7-c-ii.description: The real numbers a, b and c have mean μ and standard deviation σ. Find, with justification, the standard deviation of (a − μ)/σ, (b − μ)/σ and (c − μ)/σ.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q8-a.description: Use integration by parts to find ∫ x sin x dx.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q8-b-i.description: A window consists of a rectangle of width 2r metres and height x metres, topped by a semicircle of radius r metres. Its perimeter is 20 metres. Use the perimeter to express x in terms of r and π.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q8-b-ii.description: A window consists of a rectangle of width 2r metres and height x metres, topped by a semicircle of radius r metres. Its perimeter is 20 metres. Find, in terms of π, the value of r for which the window’s area is a maximum.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q8-c-i.description: The Maclaurin series for tan⁻¹x is x − x³/3 + x⁵/5 − x⁷/7 + … . Write down the general term of the series.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q8-c-ii.description: The Maclaurin series for tan⁻¹x is x − x³/3 + x⁵/5 − x⁷/7 + … . Use the Ratio Test to show that the series converges for |x| < 1.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q8-c-iii.description: The Maclaurin series for tan⁻¹x is x − x³/3 + x⁵/5 − x⁷/7 + … . Use π/4 = 4 tan⁻¹(1/5) − tan⁻¹(1/239) and the first three terms of the series to approximate π, correct to five decimal places.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q9-a.description: Z has a standard normal distribution. Use the tables to find z₁ such that P(Z ≥ z₁) = 0.0778.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q9-b.description: A biased die rolls a six with probability p; its other five numbers are equally likely. It is rolled with a fair die. Show that the probability of a total of 7 is independent of p.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q9-c-i.description: The mean percentage mark in the 2010 Higher Mathematics exam was 67.0%, with standard deviation 10.4%. A random sample of candidates who appealed has mean 69.3%. Investigate whether appealing candidates have similar average results to all candidates. Show that, for a sample of 25, the result is not significant at the 5% level.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q9-c-ii.description: The mean percentage mark in the 2010 Higher Mathematics exam was 67.0%, with standard deviation 10.4%. A random sample of candidates who appealed has mean 69.3%. Investigate whether appealing candidates have similar average results to all candidates. Show that, for a sample of 100, the result is significant at the 5% level.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q9-c-iii.description: The mean percentage mark in the 2010 Higher Mathematics exam was 67.0%, with standard deviation 10.4%. A random sample of candidates who appealed has mean 69.3%. Investigate whether appealing candidates have similar average results to all candidates. Find the smallest sample size for which the result is significant at the 5% level.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-a-i.description: Use the original Cayley table for the group ({a, b, c}, *): row a is c,a,b; row b is a,b,c; row c is b,c,a, in column order a,b,c. Write down the identity element.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-a-ii.description: Use the original Cayley table for the group ({a, b, c}, *): row a is c,a,b; row b is a,b,c; row c is b,c,a, in column order a,b,c. Write down the inverse of each element.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-b-i.description: The twelve rotational symmetries of a regular tetrahedron form a group G under composition. Represent symmetries as permutations of the vertices A, B, C and D. Write one element x of order 3 in permutation form, and describe the symmetry geometrically.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-b-ii.description: The twelve rotational symmetries of a regular tetrahedron form a group G under composition. Represent symmetries as permutations of the vertices A, B, C and D. Write one element y of order 2 in permutation form, and describe the symmetry geometrically.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-b-iii.description: The twelve rotational symmetries of a regular tetrahedron form a group G under composition. Represent symmetries as permutations of the vertices A, B, C and D. Choose x of order 3 and y of order 2, giving each permutation and its geometrical description. Show that x ∘ y ≠ y ∘ x.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-b-iv.description: The twelve rotational symmetries of a regular tetrahedron form a group G under composition. Represent symmetries as permutations of the vertices A, B, C and D. Choose x of order 3 and y of order 2, giving each permutation and its geometrical description. Let S = {e, x, y, x ∘ y, y ∘ x, x ∘ x}, where e is the identity. Show that S is not closed under composition.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q10-b-v.description: The twelve rotational symmetries of a regular tetrahedron form a group G under composition. Represent symmetries as permutations of the vertices A, B, C and D. Choose x of order 3 and y of order 2, giving each permutation and its geometrical description. The preceding tasks show x ∘ y ≠ y ∘ x and that S = {e, x, y, x ∘ y, y ∘ x, x ∘ x} is not closed. Let H be a subgroup of G with x and y in H. Show that H = G.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q11-a.description: An ellipse has centre (0, 0), eccentricity 1/2 and a focus at (2, 0). Find its equation.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q11-b-i.description: P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) satisfy x₁ < x₂. The slope of PQ is tan θ and its length is d. Express x₂ − x₁ and y₂ − y₁ in terms of d and θ.

maths-2011-hl-p2-q11-b-ii.description: P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) satisfy x₁ < x₂. The slope of PQ is tan θ and its length is d. The transformation f is x′ = 2x + 5y + 6, y′ = 3x + 4y + 1. Show that |f(P)f(Q)|/|PQ| = √[(2 cos θ + 5 sin θ)² + (3 cos θ + 4 sin θ)²].

maths-2011-hl-p2-q11-b-iii.description: P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) satisfy x₁ < x₂. The slope of PQ is tan θ and its length is d. The transformation f is x′ = 2x + 5y + 6, y′ = 3x + 4y + 1. The preceding part establishes |f(P)f(Q)|/|PQ| = √[(2 cos θ + 5 sin θ)² + (3 cos θ + 4 sin θ)²]. Deduce that the ratio of lengths on parallel lines is invariant under f.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-a-i.description: Aoife and Brian share a prize fund in the ratio 4 : 3. Aoife gets €56. Find the total prize fund.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-a-ii.description: Aoife and Brian share a prize fund in the ratio 4 : 3. Aoife gets €56. How much does Brian get?

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-b-i.description: A three-night hotel stay in England costs £231 sterling. €1 = £0.88 sterling. Find the cost in euro.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-b-ii.description: A three-night hotel stay in England costs £231 sterling. €1 = £0.88 sterling. This cost is 5% more than a year ago. Find the cost a year ago in euro.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-c-i.description: A faulty car speedometer reads 60 km/h when the actual speed is 57 km/h. Calculate the percentage error, correct to one decimal place.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-c-ii.description: A faulty car speedometer reads 60 km/h when the actual speed is 57 km/h. If the percentage error is the same at all speeds, find the actual speed when the speedometer reads 110 km/h. Give your answer to one decimal place.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q1-c-iii.description: A faulty car speedometer reads 60 km/h when the actual speed is 57 km/h. The percentage error is the same at all speeds. The driver expects a journey at an indicated average 80 km/h to take four hours. How long will it actually take, to the nearest minute?

maths-2011-ol-p1-q2-b-i.description: Find A, the solution set of 3x − 5 < 7, for integer x.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q2-b-ii.description: Find B, the solution set of (−2 − 3x)/4 ≤ 1, for integer x.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q2-b-iii.description: A is the integer solution set of 3x − 5 < 7; B is the integer solution set of (−2 − 3x)/4 ≤ 1. List the elements of A ∩ B.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q2-c-i.description: f(x) = x³ − 2x² + cx + d. Given f(0) = 6, find d.

maths-2011-ol-p1-q2-c-ii.description: f(x) = x³ − 2x² + cx + d. Given f(0) = 6 and f(3) = 0, find c.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q4-c-d.description: In a science experiment, Q(t) was observed at t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 seconds, giving 2.920, 2.642, 2.391, 2.163, 1.957 respectively. Q(t) = Ae^(−bt), where A and b are constants. Show that Q(t) is a constant multiple of Q(t − 1) for t ≥ 1. Find k such that Q(t + k) = ½Q(t) for all t ≥ 0, correct to two decimal places.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q5-a.description: Gold jewellery has carat rating c = 24m_g/m_t, where m_g is its gold mass and m_t its total mass. The jeweller has 147 g of 9-carat gold and 85 g of 18-carat gold. Its value is its gold content only, at €36 per gram. What is the total value of the jeweller’s stock of old jewellery?

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q5-b.description: Gold jewellery has carat rating c = 24m_g/m_t, where m_g is its gold mass and m_t its total mass. The jeweller has 147 g of 9-carat gold and 85 g of 18-carat gold. Its value is its gold content only, at €36 per gram. The jeweller wants a 21 g pendant of 15-carat gold. How many grams of 9-carat and 18-carat gold should he use?

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q5-c.description: Gold jewellery has carat rating c = 24m_g/m_t, where m_g is its gold mass and m_t its total mass. The jeweller has 147 g of 9-carat gold and 85 g of 18-carat gold. Its value is its gold content only, at €36 per gram. In the old jewellery, silver and copper masses are equal. Pure silver can be added. The new item weighs 48 g, is 15-carat, and has twice as much silver as copper. Find the copper mass in the 48 g item. Find the masses of each stock (9-carat gold, 18-carat gold and pure silver) needed to make it.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q5-d.description: Gold jewellery has carat rating c = 24m_g/m_t, where m_g is its gold mass and m_t its total mass. The jeweller has 147 g of 9-carat gold and 85 g of 18-carat gold. Its value is its gold content only, at €36 per gram. The business makes 14-carat rings averaging 5 g; each costs €135 plus its gold value. At €200 each, 20 rings sell per month. Each additional €20 reduces sales by one. Find the monthly profit in terms of x when the selling price is €(200 + 20x). Find the selling-price range for monthly profit of at least €1600.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q6-a.description: New York Lotto pays 26 annual payments, the first immediately and the last after 25 years. Payments increase by 4% each year. The advertised jackpot is their total; the cash-value option pays a smaller immediate amount. If the first payment is A, write the second, third, fourth and 26th payments in terms of A.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q6-b.description: New York Lotto pays 26 annual payments, the first immediately and the last after 25 years. Payments increase by 4% each year. The advertised jackpot is their total; the cash-value option pays a smaller immediate amount. The first payment is A. The 26 payments form a geometric series. Express the advertised jackpot in terms of A.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q6-c.description: New York Lotto pays 26 annual payments, the first immediately and the last after 25 years. Payments increase by 4% each year. The advertised jackpot is their total; the cash-value option pays a smaller immediate amount. The first payment is A. Find A, correct to the nearest dollar, for an advertised jackpot of $21.5 million.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q6-d-i-ii.description: New York Lotto pays 26 annual payments, the first immediately and the last after 25 years. Payments increase by 4% each year. The advertised jackpot is their total; the cash-value option pays a smaller immediate amount. The advertised jackpot is $21.5 million. The cash value is the total present value of the payments, using annual interest of 4.78%. Complete the table of actual amounts and present values for the first three annual payments. Express the present value of the nth annual payment in terms of n.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q6-d-iii-e.description: New York Lotto pays 26 annual payments, the first immediately and the last after 25 years. Payments increase by 4% each year. The advertised jackpot is their total; the cash-value option pays a smaller immediate amount. The advertised jackpot is $21.5 million. The cash value is the total present value of the payments, using annual interest of 4.78%. Find the cash-value prize in millions to one decimal place. The winner receives $7.9 million after tax: find the percentage tax.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-a.description: Differentiate cos²x with respect to x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-b-i.description: The equation of a curve is y = e^(−x²). Find dy/dx.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-b-ii.description: The equation of a curve is y = e^(−x²). Find the co-ordinates of the turning point of the curve.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-b-iii.description: The equation of a curve is y = e^(−x²). Determine whether this turning point is a local maximum or a local minimum.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-c-i.description: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x + 1), where x is real and x ≠ −1. Find the equations of the asymptotes of y = f(x).

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-c-ii.description: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x + 1), where x is real and x ≠ −1. P and Q are distinct points on y = f(x). The tangent at Q is parallel to the tangent at P, where P = (1, 1). Find the co-ordinates of Q.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q7-c-iii.description: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x/(x + 1), where x is real and x ≠ −1. P = (1, 1), Q is distinct from P, and the tangents at P and Q are parallel. Verify that the intersection of the asymptotes is the midpoint of [PQ].

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q8-a.description: Find the slope of the tangent to x² + y³ = x − 2 at (3, −2).

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q8-b-i.description: A curve is defined by x = (t − 1)/(t + 1) and y = −4t/(t + 1)², where t ≠ −1. Find dx/dt and dy/dt.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q8-b-ii.description: A curve is defined by x = (t − 1)/(t + 1) and y = −4t/(t + 1)², where t ≠ −1. Hence find dy/dx, and express your answer in terms of x.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q8-c-i.description: For real x excluding −1 and 0, f(x) = tan⁻¹(−x/(x + 1)) and g(x) = tan⁻¹((x + 1)/x). Show that f′(x) = −1/(2x² + 2x + 1).

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q8-c-ii.description: For real x excluding −1 and 0, f(x) = tan⁻¹(−x/(x + 1)) and g(x) = tan⁻¹((x + 1)/x). The preceding part establishes f′(x) = −1/(2x² + 2x + 1). It can be shown that f′(x) = g′(x). Based only on the derivatives, state which of the three original diagrams A, B or C represents parts of the graphs of f and g, and why each other diagram is incorrect.

maths-2011-hl-p1-project-q9-c.description: Use integration methods to establish A = πr² for the area of a disc of radius r.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q1-a.description: A random variable X follows a normal distribution with mean 20 and standard deviation 5. Find P(14 ≤ X ≤ 26).

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q1-b.description: There are 16 girls and 8 boys in a class. Half study French. The probability that a randomly selected girl studies French is 1.5 times that for a randomly selected boy. How many boys study French?

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q2-a.description: Explain, with the aid of an example, what is meant by “Correlation does not imply causality.”

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q2-b-i.description: The observations are (x, y) = (1, 11), (2, 15), (3, 17), (4, 17), (5, 15), (6, 11), shown in the table and scatter diagram. Calculate the correlation coefficient.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q2-b-ii.description: The observations are (x, y) = (1, 11), (2, 15), (3, 17), (4, 17), (5, 15), (6, 11), shown in the table and scatter diagram. What kind of relationship, if any, do the observed data suggest exists between x and y?

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q3-a.description: The co-ordinate diagram shows parallel lines j, k and l, and parallel lines m and n. Four equations are provided: x + 2y = −4; 2x − y = −4; x + 2y = 8; 2x − y = 2. Complete the table by matching four of the lines to their equations.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q3-b.description: The co-ordinate diagram shows parallel lines j, k and l, and parallel lines m and n. Four equations are provided: x + 2y = −4; 2x − y = −4; x + 2y = 8; 2x − y = 2. First match the four given equations to the lines. Hence, insert scales on the x-axis and y-axis.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q3-c.description: The co-ordinate diagram shows parallel lines j, k and l, and parallel lines m and n. Four equations are provided: x + 2y = −4; 2x − y = −4; x + 2y = 8; 2x − y = 2. First match the equations and insert scales on both axes. Hence, find the equation of the remaining line, given that its x-intercept and y-intercept are both integers.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q4-a.description: The triangles are on a square grid. P, Q, R, X and Z are grid vertices; Y lies on [PR]. Triangle PQR is an enlargement of triangle XYZ. Calculate the scale factor of the enlargement, showing your work.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q4-b.description: The triangles are on a square grid. P, Q, R, X and Z are grid vertices; Y lies on [PR]. Triangle PQR is an enlargement of triangle XYZ. By construction or otherwise, locate the centre of enlargement on the diagram.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q4-c.description: The triangles are on a square grid. P, Q, R, X and Z are grid vertices; Y lies on [PR]. Triangle PQR is an enlargement of triangle XYZ. Part (a) asks for the scale factor. Calculate |YR| in grid units.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q5.description: The line x + 3y = 20 intersects the circle x² + y² − 6x − 8y = 0 at P and Q. Find the equation of the circle that has [PQ] as diameter.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q6a.description: Prove that if three parallel lines cut off equal segments on some transversal line, then they will cut off equal segments on any other transversal line. Include a diagram, the given information, what is to be proved, a construction and the proof.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q6b.description: In the diagram, P₁Q₁, P₂Q₂ and P₃Q₃ are parallel, and Q₁P₂ and Q₂P₃ are parallel. Prove that |P₁Q₁| × |P₃Q₃| = |P₂Q₂|².

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-a-i.description: Students investigate the time between successive 20th-century earthquakes causing at least 1,000 deaths. The 115 intervals, in days, have frequencies: 0–100:31; 100–200:24; 200–300:12; 300–400:14; 400–500:8; 500–600:7; 600–700:5; 700–800:6; 800–1000:5; 1000–1300:3. Create a suitable graphical representation of the distribution.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-a-ii.description: Students investigate the time between successive 20th-century earthquakes causing at least 1,000 deaths. The 115 intervals, in days, have frequencies: 0–100:31; 100–200:24; 200–300:12; 300–400:14; 400–500:8; 500–600:7; 600–700:5; 700–800:6; 800–1000:5; 1000–1300:3. Describe the distribution, referring to its shape and estimating its median.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-a-iii.description: Students investigate the time between successive 20th-century earthquakes causing at least 1,000 deaths. The 115 intervals, in days, have frequencies: 0–100:31; 100–200:24; 200–300:12; 300–400:14; 400–500:8; 500–600:7; 600–700:5; 700–800:6; 800–1000:5; 1000–1300:3. The mean interval is 309 days and the standard deviation is 277 days. After such an earthquake occurs, explain why standard normal distribution tables cannot give the probability that the next one occurs between 100 and 200 days later.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-a-iv.description: Students investigate the time between successive 20th-century earthquakes causing at least 1,000 deaths. The 115 intervals, in days, have frequencies: 0–100:31; 100–200:24; 200–300:12; 300–400:14; 400–500:8; 500–600:7; 600–700:5; 700–800:6; 800–1000:5; 1000–1300:3. Part (iii) concerns a wait between 100 and 200 days after the previous earthquake. Based on the information so far, give the best estimate of the probability described in part (iii), and explain your reasoning.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-a-v.description: Students investigate the time between successive 20th-century earthquakes causing at least 1,000 deaths. The 115 intervals, in days, have frequencies: 0–100:31; 100–200:24; 200–300:12; 300–400:14; 400–500:8; 500–600:7; 600–700:5; 700–800:6; 800–1000:5; 1000–1300:3. Suggest a different way to analyse the database to look for patterns in the timing of earthquakes.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-b-i.description: The back-to-back histograms show magnitudes of 20th-century earthquakes causing tsunamis and not causing tsunamis. A reporter claims strong earthquakes cause tsunamis while weaker ones do not. Comment on the reporter’s statement using the diagram, and suggest a more accurate statement.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-b-ii.description: The back-to-back histograms show magnitudes of 20th-century earthquakes causing tsunamis and not causing tsunamis. A reporter claims strong earthquakes cause tsunamis while weaker ones do not. Use suitable readings from the diagram to estimate the probability that an earthquake of magnitude between 6.5 and 7.0 causes a tsunami.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-b-iii.description: The back-to-back histograms show magnitudes of 20th-century earthquakes causing tsunamis and not causing tsunamis. A reporter claims strong earthquakes cause tsunamis while weaker ones do not. Estimate the probability that at least four of the next six earthquakes of magnitude at least 7.5 cause a tsunami, assuming independence.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q7-c.description: Find the radius of the earth’s core from the diagram. The earth has radius 6.4 units, the seismic path is a circular arc of radius 29.1 units and just touches the core, and ∠AOB = 104°. One unit is 1,000 km.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q8-a-i.description: A tower has a square base of side 4 m and a pyramidal roof. A surveyor at O is 10 m horizontally from the tower. The angles of elevation to the apex and closest roof-base point are 46° and 42°; the angle of depression to the closest tower-base point is 9°. Find the vertical height of the roof.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q8-a-ii.description: A tower has a square base of side 4 m and a pyramidal roof. A surveyor at O is 10 m horizontally from the tower. The angles of elevation to the apex and closest roof-base point are 46° and 42°; the angle of depression to the closest tower-base point is 9°. Part (i) asks for the vertical roof height. Find the total area of the roof.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q8-a-iii.description: A tower has a square base of side 4 m and a pyramidal roof. A surveyor at O is 10 m horizontally from the tower. The angles of elevation to the apex and closest roof-base point are 46° and 42°; the angle of depression to the closest tower-base point is 9°. If all observed angles are subject to a possible error of ±1°, find the range of possible areas for the roof.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q8-b-i.description: Twenty-five students each measure an angle of elevation with a home-made clinometer. The readings in degrees are 24,20,22,15,70; 15,16,15,16,15; 18,16,21,21,73; 16,20,12,18,20; 18,18,14,22,18. Find what you consider the best estimate of the true angle, explaining your reasoning.

maths-2011-hl-p2-project-q8-b-ii.description: Twenty-five students each measure an angle of elevation with a home-made clinometer. The readings in degrees are 24,20,22,15,70; 15,16,15,16,15; 18,16,21,21,73; 16,20,12,18,20; 18,18,14,22,18. First choose and justify an estimate of the true angle. A teacher claims that half of students measure the angle correctly to within two degrees. Treat these students as a simple random sample and your part (i) estimate as the true angle. Is there sufficient evidence to reject the claim at the 5% significance level?

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q1-a.description: Explain what a prime number is.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q1-b.description: Express 2652 as a product of prime numbers.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q1-c.description: The number 2⁶¹ − 1 is prime. Using your calculator, or otherwise, express its value to two significant figures as a × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ a < 10 and n is natural.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q1-d.description: Part (c) asks for 2⁶¹ − 1 to two significant figures in scientific notation. Calculate this first if practising independently. Use your scientific-notation answer from part (c) to state how many digits are in the exact value of 2⁶¹ − 1.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q2-a.description: A €20,000 deposit earns 3% in the first year and 6% in the second. Interest is added at the end of each year. How much is in the account at the end of the two years?

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q2-b.description: A €20,000 deposit earns 3% in the first year and 6% in the second. Interest is added at the end of each year. Show that, to the nearest euro, the same interest is earned by investing the money for two years at 4.49% compound interest (AER).

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q3-a.description: The arithmetic sequence is Tₙ = 38 − 4n, for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, …. Write out the first three terms.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q3-b.description: The arithmetic sequence is Tₙ = 38 − 4n, for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, …. What is the first negative term?

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q3-c.description: The arithmetic sequence is Tₙ = 38 − 4n, for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, …. Find the sum of the first 15 terms.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q3-d.description: The arithmetic sequence is Tₙ = 38 − 4n, for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, …. Find n for which the sum of the first n terms is 0.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q4-b.description: Solve 5 − (3/4)x ≤ 19/8 and show the solution set on the original number line.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q5-a-i.description: z = 1 + i, where i² = −1. Find z² and z³.

maths-2011-ol-p1-project-q5-a-ii.description: z = 1 + i, where i² = −1. Verify that z⁴ = −4.

maths-2010-hl-p1-q8-c-iii.description: I = ∫ from a to b of cos(x)/(1 + sin(x)) dx and J = ∫ from a to b of sin(x)/(1 + cos(x)) dx. Show that if a + b = π/2, then I = J.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q1-a.description: Find the equation of the circle with centre (3, −4) passing through (7, −3).

maths-2010-hl-p2-q1-b-i.description: The circle has equation x² + y² − 8x − 10y + 32 = 0. Find the centre and radius of the circle.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q1-b-ii.description: The circle has equation x² + y² − 8x − 10y + 32 = 0. The line 3x + 4y + k = 0 is tangent to the circle. Find the two possible values of k.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q1-c.description: Find the equation of a circle that has y = 2x as a tangent at (2, 4) and also passes through (4, −2).

maths-2010-hl-p2-q2-a.description: A, B and C are points and O is the origin. a = 2i + 3j, b = −3i − 6j, and vector AC = vector OB. Express the position vector c in terms of i and j.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q2-b-i.description: u = 2i + j and v = −i + kj, where k is real. Express |v| and u · v in terms of k.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q2-b-ii.description: u = 2i + j and v = −i + kj, where k is real. Given cos θ = −1/√2, where θ is the angle between u and v, find the two possible values of k.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q2-c-i.description: OABC is a parallelogram with O as origin. Q is the midpoint of BC. AQ is extended to R so that QR = AQ. Lower-case letters denote position vectors. Express q in terms of a and c.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q2-c-ii.description: OABC is a parallelogram with O as origin. Q is the midpoint of BC. AQ is extended to R so that QR = AQ. Lower-case letters denote position vectors. Express vector AQ in terms of a and c.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q2-c-iii.description: OABC is a parallelogram with O as origin. Q is the midpoint of BC. AQ is extended to R so that QR = AQ. Lower-case letters denote position vectors. Show that O, C and R are collinear.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q3-a.description: The line 3x + 4y − 7 = 0 is perpendicular to ax − 6y − 1 = 0. Find a.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q3-b-i.description: The line 4x − 5y + k = 0 meets the x-axis at P and the y-axis at Q; O is the origin. Write down the coordinates of P and Q in terms of k.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q3-b-ii.description: The line 4x − 5y + k = 0 meets the x-axis at P and the y-axis at Q; O is the origin. The area of triangle OPQ is 10 square units. Find the two possible values of k.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q3-c-i.description: The transformation f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x + y and y′ = x − y. The line l has equation y = mx + c. Find the equation of f(l), the image of l under f.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q3-c-ii.description: The transformation f maps (x, y) to (x′, y′), where x′ = x + y and y′ = x − y. The line l has equation y = mx + c. Find every value of m for which f(l) makes an angle of 45° with l.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q4-a.description: Triangle PQR has area 20 cm², PQ = 10 cm and PR = 8 cm. Find the two possible values of angle QPR.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q4-b.description: Find all solutions of cos 2x = cos x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q4-c-i.description: Triangle ABC has sides a, b and c and an incircle of centre O and radius r, as shown. Show that the area of triangle ABC is ½r(a + b + c).

maths-2010-hl-p2-q4-c-ii.description: Triangle ABC has sides a, b and c and an incircle of centre O and radius r, as shown. The side lengths are a = p² + q², b = p² − q² and c = 2pq, where p and q are natural numbers with p > q. Show that this triangle is right-angled.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q4-c-iii.description: Triangle ABC has sides a, b and c and an incircle of centre O and radius r, as shown. The side lengths are a = p² + q², b = p² − q² and c = 2pq, where p and q are natural numbers with p > q. You may use the area identity ½r(a + b + c) and the right-angle result from the preceding parts. Show that the radius of the incircle is a whole number.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q5-a.description: Given tan θ = 1/3, show that tan 2θ = 3/4.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q5-b-i.description: The triangle has sides 4, 5 and 6, with angles A, B and C labelled in the original diagram. Using the cosine rule, show that cos A + cos C = 7/8.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q5-b-ii.description: The triangle has sides 4, 5 and 6, with angles A, B and C labelled in the original diagram. Show that cos(A + C) = −9/16.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q5-c-i.description: (cos A + cos B)² + (sin A + sin B)² = 2 + 2 cos(A − B). Prove the stated trigonometric identity.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q5-c-ii.description: Use the identity (cos A + cos B)² + (sin A + sin B)² = 2 + 2 cos(A − B). Hence solve (cos 4x + cos x)² + (sin 4x + sin x)² = 2 + 2√3 sin 3x for 0° ≤ x ≤ 360°.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q6-a.description: One bag has four red and six blue discs; another has five red and seven yellow discs. One disc is drawn from each. What is the probability both are red?

maths-2010-hl-p2-q6-b.description: α and β are the roots of px² + qx + r = 0. The sequence is uₙ = lαⁿ + mβⁿ for all natural n. Prove that p uₙ₊₂ + q uₙ₊₁ + r uₙ = 0 for all natural n.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q6-c.description: Six people sit at random in a row of 11 seats. How much more likely is it that all six sit together than that no two sit together?

maths-2010-hl-p2-q7-a.description: A password has four characters chosen from capital letters A–Z and digits 0–9, and starts with a letter. BA7A, C999 and DGKK are allowed; 7DCA is not. Show that there are more than a million permitted passwords.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q7-b-i.description: Karen’s English course has six novels, four plays and ten poems. The exam asks about one text of each type. She has studied four novels, three plays and seven poems. Find the probability Karen has studied all three of the texts on the exam.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q7-b-ii.description: Karen’s English course has six novels, four plays and ten poems. The exam asks about one text of each type. She has studied four novels, three plays and seven poems. Find the probability Karen has studied none of the texts on the exam.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q7-b-iii.description: Karen’s English course has six novels, four plays and ten poems. The exam asks about one text of each type. She has studied four novels, three plays and seven poems. Find the probability Karen has studied at least two of the texts on the exam.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q7-c-i.description: The real numbers a, 2a, 3a, 4a and 5a have mean μ and standard deviation σ. Express μ and σ in terms of a.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q7-c-ii.description: The real numbers a, 2a, 3a, 4a and 5a have mean μ and standard deviation σ. Hence write down the mean and standard deviation of 3a + 5, 6a + 5, 9a + 5, 12a + 5 and 15a + 5.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q8-a.description: Use integration by parts to find ∫ ln x dx.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q8-b-i.description: A rectangle is inscribed between y = 9 − x² and the x-axis as shown; p is its positive half-width. Write an expression for the area of the rectangle in terms of p.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q8-b-ii.description: A rectangle is inscribed between y = 9 − x² and the x-axis as shown; p is its positive half-width. First write the area in terms of p. Hence calculate the area of the largest possible rectangle.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q8-c-i.description: Derive the Maclaurin series for f(x) = cos x up to and including the x⁶ term.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q8-c-ii.description: Use the Maclaurin expansion of cos x derived in part (i). Hence, using sin²x = ½(1 − cos 2x), show the first three non-zero Maclaurin terms for sin²x are x² − x⁴/3 + 2x⁶/45.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q8-c-iii.description: The first three non-zero terms of sin²x are x² − x⁴/3 + 2x⁶/45. Use these terms to approximate sin²(½), as a fraction.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q9-a.description: Z has a standard normal distribution. Find P(−1 < Z ≤ 1).

maths-2010-hl-p2-q9-b-i.description: A test has 20 multiple-choice questions, each with four possible answers and exactly one correct answer. Seán guesses every answer at random. Find the probability Seán gets none answers correct. Give the answer to three decimal places.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q9-b-ii.description: A test has 20 multiple-choice questions, each with four possible answers and exactly one correct answer. Seán guesses every answer at random. Find the probability Seán gets exactly five answers correct. Give the answer to three decimal places.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q9-b-iii.description: A test has 20 multiple-choice questions, each with four possible answers and exactly one correct answer. Seán guesses every answer at random. Find the probability Seán gets four, five or six answers correct. Give the answer to three decimal places.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q9-c.description: A random sample of 50 muffins has mean weight 80 grams and standard deviation 6 grams. Form a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of muffins produced by the bakery.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-a-i.description: The operation is x ∗ y = x + y − xy. See the original printed domain and the source correction attached to the answer. Find the identity element.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-a-ii.description: The operation is x ∗ y = x + y − xy. See the original printed domain and the source correction attached to the answer. Express the inverse of x in terms of x.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-b-i.description: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition. Write down the inverses of b and d.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-b-ii.description: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition. Verify that (b ∘ d)⁻¹ = d⁻¹ ∘ b⁻¹.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-b-iii.description: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition. Write down all subgroups of G of order 2.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-b-iv.description: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition. K is the subgroup of G of order 3. List its elements.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q10-b-v.description: G is the group of the six permutations of {1, 2, 3} labelled a, b, c, d, f and g in the original table. The operation is composition. K is the subgroup of order 3. H = {1, w, w²} is a group under multiplication, where w³ = 1. Give an isomorphism from K under composition to H under multiplication, fully justifying that it is an isomorphism.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q11-a.description: Find the equation of an ellipse centred at (0, 0), with eccentricity 4/5 and major-axis length 2 units.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q11-b-i.description: f is an affine transformation and M is the midpoint of the segment AB. Show that f(M) is the midpoint of the segment joining f(A) and f(B).

maths-2010-hl-p2-q11-b-ii.description: f is an affine transformation and M is the midpoint of the segment AB. Triangle ABC has centroid G. Show that triangle f(A)f(B)f(C) has centroid f(G).

maths-2010-hl-p2-q11-c-i.description: The ellipse is x²/100 + y²/25 = 1. PQ and RS are diameters, with P = (8, 3) and R = (6, −4), as shown. Using a transformation to or from the unit circle, or otherwise, show that PQ and RS are conjugate diameters.

maths-2010-hl-p2-q11-c-ii.description: The ellipse is x²/100 + y²/25 = 1. PQ and RS are diameters, with P = (8, 3) and R = (6, −4), as shown. The preceding part establishes that these are conjugate diameters. Find the area of the parallelogram that circumscribes the ellipse at P, S, Q and R.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q1-a.description: Two events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.2, P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(A′ ∩ B) = 0.6. Complete the Venn diagram.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q1-b.description: Two events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.2, P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(A′ ∩ B) = 0.6. Find the probability that neither A nor B happens.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q1-c.description: Two events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.2, P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(A′ ∩ B) = 0.6. Find the conditional probability P(A | B).

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q1-d.description: Two events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.2, P(A ∩ B) = 0.15 and P(A′ ∩ B) = 0.6. State whether A and B are independent events and justify your answer.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q2-a.description: The back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram shows two samples. The corresponding populations are assumed identical in shape and spread. Use the Tukey quick test at the 5% significance level to test whether the two populations have the same average.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q2-b.description: The diagram shows a skewed frequency distribution with vertical lines a, b and c. Identify the mean, mode and median by inserting the relevant letters.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q3-a.description: Construct the incircle of triangle ABC using only a compass and straight edge. Show all construction lines clearly.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q3-b.description: An equilateral triangle has sides of length 2 units. Find the area of its incircle.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q4-a.description: The centre of a circle lies on x − 2y − 1 = 0. The x-axis and y = 6 are tangents. Find the equation of the circle.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q4-b.description: First find the circle whose centre lies on x − 2y − 1 = 0 and which is tangent to the x-axis and y = 6. Show that x² + y² − 6x − 12y + 41 = 0 touches the circle in part (a) externally.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q5-a.description: Solve cos(3θ) = 1/2 for θ ∈ ℝ, with θ in radians.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q5-b.description: Match all three graphs f, g and h to cos(3x), 2cos(3x) and 3cos(2x).

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q5-c.description: The same graph contains cos(3x), 2cos(3x) and 3cos(2x). Label the scales on both axes in the graph from part (b).

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q6-a.description: A(−2, 9), B(6, −6) and C(11, 6) are shown in the diagram. The line l passes through B and has equation 12x − 5y − 102 = 0. Verify that C lies on l.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q6-b.description: A(−2, 9), B(6, −6) and C(11, 6) are shown in the diagram. The line l passes through B and has equation 12x − 5y − 102 = 0. Find the slope of AB, and hence find tan(∠ABC) as a fraction.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q6-c.description: A(−2, 9), B(6, −6) and C(11, 6) are shown in the diagram. The line l passes through B and has equation 12x − 5y − 102 = 0. Find both vectors BC and BA in terms of i and j.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q6-d.description: A(−2, 9), B(6, −6) and C(11, 6) are shown in the diagram. The line l passes through B and has equation 12x − 5y − 102 = 0. Part (b) asks for the slope of AB and tan(∠ABC); part (c) asks for BC and BA. Use the dot product to find cos(∠ABC), and show that it is consistent with the answer to part (b).

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-a.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. Estimate the correlation coefficient from the diagram.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-b.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. Circle the outlier and write down both the person’s age and maximum heart rate.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-c.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. Use the line of best fit to estimate the maximum heart rate of a 44-year-old person.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-d.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. Take suitable readings from the diagram and calculate the slope of the line of best fit.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-e.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. Part (d) asks for its slope. Find the equation of the line of best fit in the form MHR = a − b × age.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-f.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. First find the best-fit equation in the form MHR = a − b × age. Compare the new rule with MHR = 220 − age. Describe how their agreement varies with age, and illustrate your answer with two examples.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q7-g.description: The scatter plot shows simulated data based on a 2001 study of the maximum heart rates of 514 adults, in beats per minute, compared with age. The original graph, best-fit line and source attribution are retained. The older rule is MHR = 220 − age; first obtain the new rule from the fitted line. In the stated exercise programme, a 65-year-old uses 75% of estimated MHR. What change does replacing the old rule with the researchers’ new rule imply?

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q8-a.description: At noon a ship is 10 km due south of a lighthouse. It travels at 15 km/h on a bearing θ = tan⁻¹(4/3). Use the original diagram; the lighthouse is the coordinate origin and the east–west line is the x-axis, with kilometres as units. Draw the coordinate axes with the lighthouse as origin, the east–west line as the x-axis and kilometres as units.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q8-b.description: At noon a ship is 10 km due south of a lighthouse. It travels at 15 km/h on a bearing θ = tan⁻¹(4/3). Use the original diagram; the lighthouse is the coordinate origin and the east–west line is the x-axis, with kilometres as units. Find the equation of the line along which the ship is moving.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q8-c.description: At noon a ship is 10 km due south of a lighthouse. It travels at 15 km/h on a bearing θ = tan⁻¹(4/3). Use the original diagram; the lighthouse is the coordinate origin and the east–west line is the x-axis, with kilometres as units. Find the shortest distance between the ship and the lighthouse during the journey.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q8-d.description: At noon a ship is 10 km due south of a lighthouse. It travels at 15 km/h on a bearing θ = tan⁻¹(4/3). Use the original diagram; the lighthouse is the coordinate origin and the east–west line is the x-axis, with kilometres as units. Part (c) asks for the shortest distance. At what time is the ship closest to the lighthouse?

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q8-e.description: At noon a ship is 10 km due south of a lighthouse. It travels at 15 km/h on a bearing θ = tan⁻¹(4/3). Use the original diagram; the lighthouse is the coordinate origin and the east–west line is the x-axis, with kilometres as units. Part (c) asks for the shortest distance. Visibility is limited to 9 km. For how many minutes in total is the ship visible from the lighthouse?

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q9a-a.description: A machine produces normally distributed aluminium-rod lengths with mean equal to its setting and standard deviation 0.2 mm. It is set to 40 mm. What is the probability that a randomly selected rod is less than 39.7 mm long?

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q9a-b.description: A machine produces normally distributed aluminium-rod lengths with mean equal to its setting and standard deviation 0.2 mm. It is set to 40 mm. Five rods are selected at random. Find the probability that at least two are less than 39.7 mm long.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q9a-c.description: A machine produces normally distributed aluminium-rod lengths with mean equal to its setting and standard deviation 0.2 mm. It is set to 40 mm. The measured lengths, in mm, are 39.5, 40.0, 39.7, 40.2, 39.8, 39.7, 40.2, 39.9, 40.1, 39.6. Use the ten measured lengths to test at the 5% significance level whether the machine setting has become inaccurate. State both hypotheses and finish with a conclusion about the machine.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q9b-a.description: Prove that if three parallel lines cut off equal segments on some transversal line, then they cut off equal segments on any other transversal line. Include the diagram, given information, statement to prove, construction and proof.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q9b-b-i.description: The roof truss has AC = 6 m and pitch 35°. AD = DE = EC and AF = FB = BG = GC. Use the original complete truss diagram. Calculate AB in metres, correct to two decimal places.

maths-2010-hl-p2-project-q9b-b-ii.description: The roof truss has AC = 6 m and pitch 35°. AD = DE = EC and AF = FB = BG = GC. Use the original complete truss diagram. Part (i) asks for AB to two decimal places. Calculate the total length of timber required to make the truss.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q1-a.description: Express 40 metres as a fraction of 1 kilometre. Give your answer in its simplest form.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q1-b-i.description: Calculate (57.6 + 80.44) ÷ (1.3 × 10⁴), correct to three decimal places.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q1-b-ii.description: An importer buys an item for £221 sterling when €1 = £0.85 sterling, then sells it at a profit of 14% of cost price. Calculate, in euro, the price for which the importer sells the item.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q1-c-i.description: What sum of money invested at 5% per annum compound interest will amount to €8682 in three years? Give the answer to the nearest euro.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q1-c-ii.description: €P is invested at r% per annum compound interest. The first-year interest is €220 and the second-year interest is €228.80. Calculate r and P.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q2-a.description: Find the natural numbers x satisfying 2(3 + 4x) ≤ 22.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q2-b.description: Solve simultaneously for x and y: 2x − y = 1 and x² − xy = −6.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q2-c-i.description: Show by division that 3x + 1 is a factor of 3x³ + 4x² − 89x − 30.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q2-c-ii.description: Part (i) asks you to show by division that 3x + 1 is a factor. Hence, or otherwise, solve 3x³ + 4x² − 89x − 30 = 0.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q3-a.description: Given 3(b + a) = t(6 − a), calculate a when t = 3 and b = −4.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q3-b.description: Solve 5(x + 1)² = 2(x + 1) + 5, giving both answers correct to two decimal places.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q3-c-i.description: 2 + √3 is a root of x² − 4x + c = 0, where c is real. Find c and write down the other root.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q3-c-ii.description: The equation x² + 10x + k = 0 has equal roots. Find the real number k and the value of each root.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q4-a.description: Given i² = −1, simplify (4 + 2i)(3 − i) and write the answer as x + yi, where x and y are real.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q4-b-i.description: Let u = 4 + 3i and w = 6 − 8i. Find the real number k such that |u| = k|w|.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q4-b-ii.description: Let u = 4 + 3i and w = 6 − 8i. Express w/u in the form x + yi.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q4-c.description: Let z = a + bi, with a and b real. Find a and b for which 3z − 10i = (2 − 3i)z.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-a.description: The first term is 4 and the common ratio is 0.5. Write down the first five terms of the geometric sequence.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-b-i.description: In an arithmetic series, the first term is 6 and the fifth term is 22. Find d, the common difference.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-b-ii.description: In an arithmetic series, the first term is 6 and the fifth term is 22. Part (i) asks for the common difference. Find T₁₄, the fourteenth term.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-b-iii.description: In an arithmetic series, the first term is 6 and the fifth term is 22. Earlier parts ask for d and T₁₄. Find S₂₀, the sum of the first twenty terms.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-c-i.description: In a geometric series, the fourth term is 9 and the seventh term is 243. Find r, the common ratio.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-c-ii.description: In a geometric series, the fourth term is 9 and the seventh term is 243. Part (i) asks for r. Find a, the first term.

maths-2010-ol-p1-q5-c-iii.description: In a geometric series, the fourth term is 9 and the seventh term is 243. Earlier parts ask for r and a. Find S₈, the sum of the first eight terms.
